#5153. Bitcoin Rebounds After Democratic Midterm Sweep, But Crypto Faces Tougher Fight in Washington

Bitcoin Rebounds After Democratic Midterm Sweep, But Crypto Faces Tougher Fight in Washington

Bitcoin and Ethereum recovered Wednesday after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections, despite the results likely making the crypto industry's push for friendlier federal rules more difficult.

The crypto market recovery, in technical terms, appears to be more a natural bounce, and in line with expectations, instead of a trend reversal or a FOMO-driven spike. The overnight selloff also reversed as U.S. stock futures bounced back, making it hard to pin the recovery on politics alone.

Bitcoin briefly hit a six-week low before a bounce that took it back to just above $80,000 once again, above its average price of the last 50 days, which is a solid bullish sign after weeks of bearish correction.

Ethereum, meanwhile, spiked 7% to $2,434, while U.S. stocks on the whole jumped around 1.6%, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average leading the way with a 2.5% rally.

Analysts who spoke to Decrypt said the Democratic sweep had largely been priced into crypto markets before election night. A rebound in Bitcoin therefore says less about investors welcoming the election result than about how much bad news they were already expecting.

The industry has spent more than $300 million supporting crypto-friendly candidates from both parties across the 2024 and 2026 election cycles. About $176 million went toward more than 100 races this year alone.

That spending was aimed partly at getting legislation through Congress that would give digital asset businesses clearer rules. The Clarity Act, a major piece of that effort, would define how federal regulators oversee different types of crypto assets and trading activity.

The bill was in trouble before Tuesday's election. Senators voted 49-50 against advancing it in September, falling short of the 60 votes needed to move past a procedural hurdle. That was not a final vote on the legislation, but it stopped the measure from reaching a full debate.

Negotiations had already run into disputes over restrictions on government officials' crypto business interests and the treatment of rewards paid on stablecoins, tokens designed to hold a fixed value. President Donald Trump's personal and family crypto ventures became a particular point of conflict for Democratic lawmakers.

Democratic control of Congress makes a quick return to the same legislative deal less likely, but it does not automatically undo what the industry secured under Trump. His administration has eased enforcement, established a strategic Bitcoin reserve and overseen the passage of a federal stablecoin law.

The distinction matters more for exchanges, token issuers, and other firms seeking clear legal permissions than for Bitcoin's day-to-day price. Analysts told Decrypt that liquidity, interest rates and investment flows still exert a stronger influence on the cryptocurrency itself.

The broader crypto market has shed roughly $300 billion over the past month, bringing its total value to about $2.67 trillion. Rising borrowing costs and worries about returns on artificial intelligence investments have pushed traders toward less risky assets like bonds or gold.

Major Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which offer exposure to the asset through traditional brokerage accounts, recorded $215 million in net withdrawals in October. That brought their year-to-date net outflows to $1.84 billion.

The new Congress takes office in January 2027. Unless lawmakers revive the Clarity Act before the current session ends, the industry will need to start a new legislative effort with Democrats controlling both chambers.

#5152. Core Scientific (CORZ) to Exit Bitcoin Mining by Year-End as Colocation Hits $215 Million

Core Scientific will complete its exit from bitcoin mining by year-end and enter 2027 as a pure-play high-density colocation provider, management said on Thursday’s third-quarter earnings call, capping a pivot that has already cut the company’s mining fleet nearly in half.

Chief Financial Officer Jim Nygaard told investors the company expects to “complete the wind-down during the fourth quarter.” Chief Executive Officer Adam Sullivan put the same end date more bluntly: “We expect to complete our exit from Bitcoin mining by year end.” The comments landed alongside a results release filed with the SEC that shows how far the shift has already gone.

Colocation revenue climbed nearly 60% sequentially to $215.4 million in the quarter ended Sept. 30, the earnings exhibit shows. Digital asset self-mining revenue fell to $12.3 million, down about 79% from $57.4 million a year earlier. Hosted mining for third parties added just $5.2 million. Of $232.9 million in total revenue, colocation now accounts for roughly 92%.

Self-mining posted a $7.5 million gross loss in the quarter. Colocation gross profit was $128.4 million, a 60% margin. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled sequentially to $133.6 million, with the margin expanding to 57% from 25%.

Nygaard said Core Scientific had nearly 50% fewer miners online at the end of September than at year-end 2025. The company has been repurposing power and floor space under long-term customer agreements for AI and high-performance computing workloads, a process its investor materials describe as continuing “as circumstances allow.”

That path is not unique among public miners. Peers have been selling bitcoin and leasing campuses to AI tenants, and research notes have flagged a widening funding gap between those that can finance data center builds and those that cannot.

Core Scientific is billing for 485 megawatts of colocation capacity as of Sept. 30 — up 90 MW in the quarter — representing more than $700 million in average annualized colocation GAAP revenue. The remaining roughly 100 MW under its CoreWeave buildout is in commissioning and expected to start recognizing revenue over the next few months, Sullivan said.

Beyond CoreWeave’s contracted 590 MW, Core Scientific has 530 MW under an AMD-backed agreement across five campuses, with initial delivery targeted for the first half of 2027 and full delivery by the end of 2028. Together, the two relationships cover about 1.1 GW. Once fully delivered and billing, management expects that portfolio alone to generate $1.8 billion in average annual run-rate revenue and $1.6 billion in net operating income.

Bitcoin is almost gone from the books. Digital assets stood at $2.7 million on Sept. 30, down from $49.7 million three months earlier and $222 million at year-end 2025. Earlier this year, Core Scientific was still adding coins even as it sold into the pivot; that chapter is effectively closed.

The mining exit has already carried a cash cost. A $41.9 million loss on contract termination booked in the second quarter reflects the decision to end a Block/Proto mining chip supply agreement. Liquidity ended the third quarter at about $1.7 billion, including roughly $800 million in cash, after heavy capital spending on AMD sites and the Polaris acquisition.

Sullivan framed the wind-down as simplifying the business toward “more attractive long-term growth opportunities.” Nygaard added that starting 2027 with a “very clean P&L” — one without mining in the numbers — should give investors a clearer look at a true colocation run-rate.

The test now is whether Core Scientific turns the last machines off on schedule in the fourth quarter, and whether the AMD financing package lands in time to keep that clean P&L growing.

Samsung's Stablecoin Account is now live in Samsung Wallet, allowing eligible Galaxy users in the United States to buy, hold and transfer USDC on Solana, according to a statement released Thursday.

Samsung first announced the feature on Oct. 7, with the launch originally expected in the last week of that month.

Around 82 million Galaxy devices in the U.S. are compatible with the service, according to the release. Users must be at least 18 years old, have a Samsung Account and own a compatible device running Android 13 or later. New York residents are excluded.

"For a decade, stablecoins have proved the technology works," Solana Foundation President Lily Liu said. "What they lacked was a way to reach the mainstream."

Users can send USDC to another Samsung Wallet user or a compatible external crypto wallet without paying a Samsung transfer fee. Eligible users can also send money to qualifying bank accounts in more than 60 countries, where recipients may receive local currency, with fees varying by destination.

Licensed stablecoin custodian and infrastructure provider Bastion handles the stablecoin accounts and transfer infrastructure, while Coinbase holds the USDC as its sub-custodian through Coinbase Prime Vault.

Coinbase was already working with Samsung before this launch. In October 2025, Samsung expanded its Coinbase partnership to let U.S. Galaxy users fund Coinbase accounts with Samsung Pay.

Samsung's new Stablecoin Account feature lets users access USDC without installing a separate crypto app or managing private keys themselves. The firm said it also expects to explore online and in-store stablecoin payments, and expansion to additional markets, subject to local regulation.

"Stablecoins have the potential to make moving money around the world faster and easier, and we want Galaxy users to be able to take advantage of that without having to navigate the complexity of traditional crypto tools," said Woncheol Chai, EVP and Head of the Digital Wallet Team at the Mobile eXperience (MX) Business at Samsung Electronics.

#5143. Tech, AI Stocks Split After Democratic Sweep: Microsoft Jumps, Tesla and Nvidia Tank

Tech, AI Stocks Split After Democratic Sweep: Microsoft Jumps, Tesla and Nvidia Tank

Technology stocks delivered a mixed performance Wednesday after Democrats swept the U.S. midterm elections, with investors weighing the prospect of tougher artificial intelligence regulation against expectations that a divided government could limit major policy changes.

The Nasdaq-100 climbed 1.14% to 28,500, recovering from an overnight selloff that briefly pushed index futures down more than 2%.

But beneath the broader market rebound, individual technology stocks told sharply different stories.

Microsoft jumped 6.01% to $552.32, while Google parent Alphabet rose 4.63% to $292.99, according to intraday charts reviewed Wednesday.

While software stocks jumped, hardware stocks corrected to the downside. AI chipmaking giant Nvidia fell 2.19% to $202.17, Tesla dropped 3.61% to $384.10, and Intel lost 5.80% to $57.04.

That said, none has yet shown a heavy bearish trend. Even Nvidia, which is going through the most obvious price correction, remains bullish on the longer trend as the prices test a weak support near the $200 price zone.

Bitcoin also recovered strongly, trading around $80,512, up 4.12% in the day, after an initial election-related selloff.

The conflicting moves reflect the uncertainty over what Democratic control of Congress will mean for technology companies that have benefited from the Donald Trump administration's approach to deregulation.

According to Reuters, investors are particularly concerned about greater scrutiny of AI data centers—the hardware camps of the AI industry—following Democratic victories in states such as Texas and Georgia, where large infrastructure projects have become politically contentious.

The AI sector was already facing questions over enormous infrastructure spending and whether those investments would generate adequate returns.

One of Wednesday's biggest losers was Trump Media & Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social.

Shares plunged 14.29% to $5.10, extending a decline that had been underway long before Democrats secured control of Congress.

The stock had already lost approximately 55% of its value year-to-date before Tuesday's vote.

Technical indicators show traders had been bearish on the stock for months. Trump Media has been in a technical pattern that traders refer to as a “death cross” since March 2025, and has lost nearly 90% of its market cap since its 2024 cap. A death cross happens when the average price of the last 200 days becomes greater than that of the last 50 days, suggesting the asset is losing value way too quickly.

The Nasdaq-100's recovery is encouraging for technology bulls, but the index remains well below its October highs above 31,000. The 28,000 area represents an immediate support zone, while a move back above 29,000 would strengthen the short-term recovery.

Bitcoin's recovery above $80,000 offers another indication that risk appetite has not disappeared entirely.

Still, Wednesday's split between technology winners and losers suggests investors are becoming increasingly selective about their exposure to the AI boom—and the political risks surrounding it.

#5142. Bitcoin Price Trades Near $76,000 as Nasdaq Tumbles into Correction

Bitcoin price traded near $76,000 on Thursday afternoon, down more than 5% on the day after sliding through the mid-$75,000s as a Nasdaq-led selloff in chip and AI stocks deepened into a formal correction and forced out more than $1 billion in leveraged bets, Bitcoin Magazine Pro data shows.

The afternoon session extended the morning crash that had already erased overnight gains above $80,000. Bitcoin briefly tested support near $75,400 before stabilizing just under $76,000 into the final hour of U.S. cash trading.

Bitcoin near $75,900 in afternoon trade, on track for its biggest single-day slide since June. The move undid Wednesday’s short-squeeze bounce in a single session. Traders who bought the midterm rebound with borrowed money were the first forced out when stocks cracked at the open, and the bitcoin price never regained the $77,000 area that held as morning support.

Wall Street set the tone. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5% on Thursday and dropped into correction territory, more than 10% below the record close it set last month, CNBC reported. The S&P 500 lost roughly 4%, and the Dow shed more than 1,600 points.

Semiconductors led the rout. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank about 11%, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF posted its biggest one-day drop since March 2020. Nvidia and Broadcom each fell around 9%, Qualcomm lost about 9% and Tesla dropped about 11%.

Investors are pricing in a slower AI data-center buildout under a Democratic Congress. Traders fear construction pauses and tighter financing for neoclouds, a risk that has weighed on chip and infrastructure names since the midterm results. Analysts told CNBC that the $1.2 trillion of AI capital spending forecast for next year is now being reworked.

Bitcoin has moved with that AI-heavy complex for most of the year. Miners that sold bitcoin to fund data centers are now caught in both trades, so political risk on power and construction hits the same names that used to trade mainly on the bitcoin price.

Forced selling kept the bitcoin price under pressure into the afternoon. Roughly $1.08 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, including about $954 million in long bets, as futures markets unwound positions built during Wednesday’s short squeeze.

Nearly $900 million of that wipeout came in a roughly four-hour stretch after the U.S. open, turning a stock-led break into a cascade of margin calls. Ether fell below $2,300 as the same leverage flushed out.

Crypto equities followed. Strategy (MSTR), Coinbase (COIN) and Circle (CRCL) each fell more than 10%, and bitcoin miners dropped as much as 20%. Keel Infrastructure (KEEL), which sold its entire bitcoin treasury for $192 million, slid about 20%. CleanSpark (CLSK), Cipher (CIFR) and TeraWulf (WULF) each lost more than 12%.

The next test is Friday’s October jobs report, then October CPI on Nov. 10 and the Fed’s Dec. 9 decision. Policy risk is building too, with House Democrats drafting their own market structure bill ahead of taking the committees in January.

Traders are watching whether the bitcoin price can hold the mid-$75,000 area that served as support on election night and several times since August. A clean break would leave bitcoin with room to run lower, near its weakest levels in months and put the September low back in view.

Options markets have been quiet into the jobs print, but the cash market is not. Volume stayed elevated through the afternoon as stocks and crypto sold together rather than against each other.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $75,900.

The firm plans to offer European-style bitcoin and ether options with maturities of up to one year if its application is approved.

Institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital has filed an application to register a swap dealer with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission as it looks to expand its institutional crypto options business.

The application was submitted to the National Futures Association through Anchorage Digital Swap Dealer, LLC, according to a statement shared exclusively with The Block.

Anchorage is now awaiting registration while the NFA reviews its application. CEO and co-founder Nathan McCauley offered no estimate of when that process might finish, but said the company would share further updates as appropriate. "We aren't in a position to speculate on timing," he told The Block.

If the application is approved, McCauley said Anchorage Digital Swap Dealer expects to offer European-style options on bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) and ether Ethereum (ETH), with maturities ranging up to one year. The firm intends to add more products later, he added, subject to its own approval process and regulatory requirements.

McCauley said that once registration is complete, institutional clients would be able to trade digital asset derivatives with a CFTC-registered counterparty alongside use of Anchorage Digital's existing custody and other services.

Much of Anchorage's existing options business growth has come from public companies holding bitcoin and ether on their balance sheets, the firm said in the statement, while asset managers and funds using options to manage their exposure have also contributed. McCauley would not disclose specific trading volumes or growth figures when asked by The Block, and declined to explain how Anchorage had previously arranged options trades for clients.

"What we can say is that institutional demand for regulated access to digital asset derivatives continues to grow, and establishing a dedicated swap dealer entity is part of how we're building the infrastructure to meet it," he said.

Anchorage Digital Bank, N.A. became the first federally chartered digital asset bank in 2021 and is regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The swap dealer entity would face CFTC requirements for capital, risk management, and margin, using the same framework the Dodd-Frank Act applied to the banks for interest rate, credit, and FX markets, the firm said.

"It will bring our options business under the same federal framework as the dealers they already face," McCauley said in the statement.

In March, Anchorage Digital added collateral management to its Atlas platform, including 24/7 monitoring and automated margin calls for loans, derivatives, and other institutional transactions, The Block reported at the time. It also acquired Securitize's wealth management unit in December to expand its federally regulated crypto services for registered investment advisors.

#5137. What Is x402? How AI Agents Pay With Crypto

What Is x402? How AI Agents Pay With Crypto

Nobody really built the web with payments in mind. Early HTTP specifications included a status code, 402 "Payment Required", that was reserved for a future system of online payments. Then it sat unused for about 30 years. Payments were slow and expensive, and they needed accounts, card details and middlemen who could reverse charges. None of that works for a small payment made by software.

That gap matters more now because AI agents are starting to browse, call APIs and buy services for their users. An agent can't fill in a checkout form or sign up for a monthly plan for every tool it uses. Cloudflare says more than half of internet traffic is now non-human, and it reports seeing a billion HTTP 402 responses on its network every day.

x402 is an attempt to finally give the internet a native way to pay. This guide covers what it is, how it works, who backs it, and whether there's a token involved.

The 402 "Payment Required" code has been in the HTTP standard since the 1990s. It was set aside "for future use", and x402 is the first big effort to actually use it.

x402 is an open payment standard built on top of HTTP, the protocol that moves data around the web. Coinbase launched it in May 2025 with partners including AWS, Anthropic, Circle and NEAR. It lets APIs, apps and AI agents pay for services in stablecoins as part of an ordinary web request.

x402 is not a blockchain and it is not a coin. It's a set of rules: message formats, headers and a request-and-response flow that any server or client can follow. Payments are mostly made in USDC, Circle's dollar-backed stablecoin, with Coinbase's Ethereum layer-2 network Base as the main settlement chain. The protocol works with any chain, though, and it now supports Solana, Polygon, Arbitrum and others, as well as traditional card payments.

On April 2, 2026, the Linux Foundation announced it was launching the x402 Foundation, with Coinbase contributing the protocol and companies including Microsoft, Google, Visa and Mastercard expressing initial support. The new x402 Foundation became fully operational on July 14, 2026, and now stewards the protocol under vendor-neutral governance.

We are excited to introduce x402–a new open source payments protocol built on HTTP rails.

Let’s break it down: pic.twitter.com/9PNI49NK7A

— Coinbase Developer Platform🛡️ (@CoinbaseDev) May 6, 2025

x402 works through a short handshake inside a normal web request:

Most of the onchain work is done by a facilitator, a service that verifies payments and settles them on the blockchain so sellers don't have to run their own crypto setup. On EVM chains, x402 uses EIP-3009, a standard that lets someone transfer tokens by signing a permission instead of sending a transaction themselves. This means the buyer doesn't need to hold ETH for gas.

x402's main pitch is very small payments made by machines. Settlement on Base takes seconds and costs well under a cent, so it makes sense to pay fractions of a cent for a single API call. There's no sign-up, no API key and no subscription. The agent just pays and gets what it asked for.

Adoption has grown quickly. Coinbase released x402 V2 in December 2025, which added wallet-based identity so agents don't have to pay again on every call, automatic service discovery and support for more chains. In May 2026 it added batch settlement, where agents hand sellers signed vouchers that can be settled in bulk. x402 had processed more than 196 million transactions across 12 chains as of November 1, 2026, settling more than $42 million in total, according to Fireblocks, which cited data from tracker agenteconomy.to. Coinbase says more than 97% of onchain agent transactions in Q2 2026 used x402.

It's worth noting, however, that more than half of x402's lifetime transactions came from a two-month frenzy in late 2025, when traders ran automated scripts to mint and sell PING, a token issued through x402, according to Fireblocks. Activity has since settled at a much lower level: in October 2026, x402 processed 5.1 million transactions worth about $274,000.

No. x402 is a protocol, not a cryptocurrency, and it has no official native token. Payments are made in existing stablecoins, mostly USDC. Speculative "x402" tokens have appeared on various chains, but none of them is issued or backed by Coinbase or the x402 Foundation. Be very wary of any token that claims to be the official x402 coin.

To use x402, an agent or app needs a wallet holding a supported stablecoin on a supported network, usually USDC on Base. USDC is widely available on major exchanges including Coinbase, Kraken and Binance. Coinbase lets users send USDC straight to Base. Developers can also use Coinbase Developer Platform wallets or Circle Wallets to give their agents funds, and set spending limits to keep those agents under control.

The x402 Foundation is growing fast. It had 40 member organizations when it became operational in July 2026, and its member list has since grown to 57, including Visa, Mastercard, American Express, PayPal, Google, Shopify, Circle, Stripe and AWS. Michael Hursta became the foundation's executive director on October 1, 2026.

x402 isn't the only option, though. The Agentic Commerce Protocol, an open standard developed by Stripe and OpenAI, and Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol are competing for a role in agent payments, even though Stripe and Visa are also premier members of the x402 Foundation.

Stripe has also co-developed the Machine Payments Protocol with payments blockchain Tempo. Like x402, MPP uses the HTTP 402 code to let agents pay for services, but adds session-based billing so agents can pay as they go rather than settling every request onchain.

Since June 2026, it has also supported x402 payments. The big open question is whether x402's huge transaction counts turn into steady, real commerce. If they do, the payment code that sat unused for 30 years could end up carrying much of the AI economy's payments.

Denim retires Flashblocks, adds millisecond-resolution timestamps, and updates B20 transfer and compliance controls.

Base's fourth mainnet upgrade, Denim, is live, with the Coinbase-incubated Layer 2 now producing a full canonical block every 200 milliseconds, or five per second, the project said in a statement shared with The Block on Thursday.

The upgrade also introduces millisecond-resolution timestamps for smart contracts, alongside new transfer protections and compliance controls for tokens using Base's B20 standard.

Base said the upgrade retires Flashblocks and changes how the pending block tag works, making block production "simpler, more consistent, and more reliable." Each block now follows its parent exactly 200 milliseconds later, with the protocol enforcing the interval rather than relying on the sequencer's clock.

Applications that previously relied on Flashblocks must migrate to standard canonical block subscriptions, according to the statement.

"Base’s north star is to bring the world onchain, starting with trading, financing, and payments," the statement read. "Those use cases need a chain that updates state often and lets builders reason about time precisely."

According to the statement, the upgrade also introduces BaseTime, which gives smart contracts access to Unix timestamps in milliseconds. Ethereum-compatible block.timestamp remains unchanged at whole-second resolution, while new RPC fields provide millisecond timestamps for blocks, transactions, and logs.

Denim also introduces reusable compliance policies through a NOT operator and extends transfer-executor restrictions to direct transfers. It also blocks transfers, mints and seizures that send tokens to the token contract's own address, Base said.

The upgrade follows Azul, Beryl and Cobalt, Base's first three independent upgrades since its 2023 launch. Azul introduced a new client stack and multiproof system, while Beryl brought the B20 token standard. Cobalt added conditional transactions and expanded B20 compliance features.

#5131. Canton Coin Gets SEC Nod as Wall Street Tokenization Heats Up

Canton Coin Gets SEC Nod as Wall Street Tokenization Heats Up

The blockchain behind Wall Street’s newest tokenization service just got a regulatory nod for its native token.

The SEC’s Division of Corporation Finance said in a letter dated Tuesday that it views Canton Coin, the native token of the Canton Network, as a “digital commodity” under the agency’s March interpretation of how securities laws apply to crypto.

Agency staff also said they won’t recommend enforcement action if Canton’s validators and application providers mint the token programmatically without registering it.

The relief comes a week after the Depository Trust & Clearing Corp. launched a tokenization service that runs on Canton and DTCC’s own private network, letting firms convert DTC-held stocks and Treasuries into tokens. Morgan Stanley said Tuesday that it was among the first banks to use the service.

SEC staff pointed to two representations from Canton’s lawyers. The first is that the token derives its value from the network’s programmatic operation and from supply and demand, rather than from the managerial efforts of others.

The second is that the network has no “central party.” Canton Coin launched without an initial coin offering or premine, and tokens were initially earned only by running network infrastructure and applications, according to a statement from Canton. Canton’s request letter was dated Oct. 30, four days before staff responded.

The letter has limits, though, as it reflects only staff’s position on enforcement, not a legal conclusion, and rests on the facts Canton presented, the SEC noted.

“Financial institutions need confidence in both the technology they use and the economic model that supports it,” said Yuval Rooz, CEO of Digital Asset, which created the Canton Network.

Canton said the letter is the first relief of its kind since the SEC published its March interpretive release, which found that most crypto assets aren’t securities. It’s also the first since the agency’s August Regulation Crypto Assets proposal.

The decision fits a broader shift since the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate in September, with the SEC and CFTC taking the lead on crypto rules. SEC Chair Paul Atkins said in July the agency was ready to act if Congress didn’t, and the SEC recently proposed rules on how advisers and funds hold crypto.

Digital Asset raised $355 million earlier this year from Wall Street firms and a sovereign wealth fund.

#5129. She Had a Bad Day and Consulted a Psychic. It Destroyed Her Life.

Intuitive practices have brought comfort to millions—but for some, it has opened the door to predators who weaponize belief, hope, and the search for healing.

IN EARLY 2024, a young Los Angeles musician who was down on her luck met with the FBI. She had a story that, at first, seemed unbelievable.

Nine months earlier, her career faltering and her morale low, she was approached one night by a psychic. The psychic said she could see that something was bothering her and offered to do a palm reading. The reading showed spiritual blockages hanging over the musician’s life, and the psychic said they would need to work together closely to clear them.

The musician gave the psychic thousands of dollars, the amounts increasing over time, and even bought cars for her and her family. At the psychic’s instruction, the musician lied to her own family, extracting what she could from them. When that wasn’t enough, the psychic put her to work. But now, confused and desperate, and overwhelmed by how she had even ended up in this situation in the first place, the musician needed to tell someone what had happened to her.

When the FBI ran the psychic’s name in their system, they discovered a familiar narrative of victimization had played out at least once before. Gina Rita Russell—psychic hustler, skilled manipulator, and pill-popping madame—was already on the FBI’s radar. And the story that put her there, beginning more than a decade earlier, was wilder than anyone could have imagined.

ONE NIGHT IN the fall of 2009, Jill Smith* was walking home through the streets of New York City, her self-esteem at an all-time low. Smith, 24, had just lost her job and gone through a devastating breakup. She felt vulnerable and rudderless, unable to launch her adult life. She’d been crying herself to sleep every night. When she passed a psychic storefront in the West Village, Gina Rita Russell was sitting outside at a small table. “Come for a reading,” Russell called out warmly. Smith declined politely, but Russell was persistent. So Smith took a seat and handed over $40.

Russell described herself as a “spiritual guider.” She peered into Smith’s palm, holding it in her own plump hands, and said she could see why Smith’s life was uncomfortably stalled. Even worse, she could see more bad things down the road. Smith needed Russell’s help, and fast. They would have to do “the work” to clear the mystical clouds hanging over Smith’s future, “driving the demons out” together. For the first time in a while, Smith’s despair lightened. She felt relieved that Russell wanted to help her.

What began as a cautious friendship at a rough time in a young woman’s life soon morphed into a nightmare. Over the next eight years, Russell would push Smith to abandon relationships, walk away from her budding career, and engage in degrading acts to clear what she was told was a malignant hex. And then, when the spell was finally broken, Smith would face a new uphill battle common to victims of trafficking: trying to persuade the courts that she wasn’t a coconspirator but a victim of forces that even she struggled to explain.

GROWING INTEREST IN “spiritual wellness” is driving the purchase of shiny little crystals and the borrowing of chants from Eastern traditions, plus plenty of yoga-and-gratitude retreats in places all over the world. But as part of this trend, some women are also leaning on psychics and other intuitive practitioners.

According to recent Pew research, 30 percent of Americans now consult astrology, tarot cards, or fortune tellers at least once a year. For women under 50, 43 percent “believe in astrology,” while only 27 percent of women 50 and over do. Eight percent of women say they rely at least a little on astrology, tarot cards, or fortune tellers to make big life decisions. Psychics are now ubiquitous, from small storefronts in one-stoplight towns to psychic influencers on Instagram with hundreds of thousands of followers. In November, Oprah had a psychic medium on her podcast discussing how to communicate with dead relatives. It can all be in good fun and perhaps even offer a bit of clarity. But at other times, it can veer into a form of exploitation.

In Jenkintown, Pennsylvania, a man-woman team with multiple fortune-telling charges against them allegedly fleeced a woman of more than $600,000, convincing her that they needed the money to lift a curse (their court cases are pending). A mother and daughter in Australia were recently arrested for allegedly running a $46 million psychic scam in which they told victims to sign over loans so they could use their powers to make the victims rich. And a woman in Toronto was allegedly scammed out of almost $8,000 by a Texas psychic she met on TikTok following the death of her stepfather. She was eager for guidance, and the cost of readings escalated quickly. “She would say I need more money to get rid of all this negativity—like, I need to fix you,” the woman said in describing the psychic to a reporter.

In some rare cases, exploitation can go far beyond theft, forcing victims into previously unimaginable acts. These relationships often start with grooming—the victim being offered kindness and attention—and then quickly shift into one-sided demands. The dynamics of control and manipulation depend on a power imbalance, and when the potential perpetrator is in a nontraditional form of authority with fewer guardrails in place, such as psychics and gurus, there may be a higher risk factor. Soon, victims may find themselves isolated, their resources depleted and their sense of reality in serious question.

“The exploiter is very intentional and thoughtful about identifying what that person needs the most and offering it to them, training them to trust them, to believe in them,” says Korin Hoffman Arkin, director of survivor care and engagement for Polaris, a national anti-trafficking organization. “So then when [an exploiter] starts asking for things that are maybe not so wonderful, it’s confusing. It starts out small and starts to build.”

While these stories might seem far-fetched, experts say that anyone can succumb to sophisticated manipulation tactics and the power of a trauma bond between victims and their tormentors. A false sense of security, of believing that one is invulnerable, creates its own risks, explains Laura Dryjanska, an associate professor at Rosemead School of Psychology of Biola University. “All of a sudden, you’re in much more danger because you’re not street smart,” she says. “People don’t realize that those psychological bonds can be much stronger than someone physically chained to a bed.”

SMITH WASN’T SOMEONE who seemed poised to veer off the tracks. She had been raised by supportive parents in upper-middle-class comfort in Long Island, New York, and earned a 3.49 GPA in theater production and design at Ithaca College. She didn’t smoke and only drank occasionally; her friends in college called her “Mom” because, mature beyond her years, she took care of everyone. After graduating from college in 2006, Smith looked for work as a designer, stylist, and wardrobe supervisor. She was thrilled when she landed a job on the soap opera Guiding Light. Smith, who has long chestnut hair and a toothy smile, was finding her feet in the big city, dealing with the exhilarating victories and demoralizing setbacks of early adulthood, impatient to live up to her promise. And then she met Russell.

Russell was just 24 when she beckoned Smith, and her background couldn’t have been more different. Her parents were Roma, a traditionally nomadic ethnic group from Eastern Europe, and she never attended school and is functionally illiterate. (As an adult, she would communicate by text using audio commands.) According to Russell, she and her siblings were forced at a young age by their parents, who were frequently violent, to support the family by selling trinkets on the streets and performing bogus psychic readings. By 15, already getting drunk and smoking marijuana, she says she was forced by her father into an informal marriage with her third cousin, Robert. Russell gave birth to the first of their four children at 16—though she eventually lost custody to Robert’s parents as she slid into multiple addictions.

The world had been kind to Smith, and she was brimming with trust. Russell had been primed for survival, trusting no one and empathizing with few. When Russell and Smith crossed paths, Russell wasn’t looking to help her; she needed a mark. But she framed her involvement in Smith’s life as an emergency intervention born of her concern. Did Smith have a way to get her hands on some money, fast? When Smith divulged her job loss, Russell encouraged her to apply for more jobs, stroking her ego like an old friend. Though Russell and Smith were roughly the same age, there was something maternal in her round face and soft, dark features. Russell had been groomed by her parents to understand how to win someone’s confidence, the gradual coaxing of attachment with the express purpose of betrayal. As the weeks grew into months, Russell turned herself into someone, maybe the only person, Smith could confide in.

Soon, with Russell’s encouragement, Smith got a new job, and they celebrated together. But it wasn’t enough money to save Smith, spiritually speaking. What started out as a $40 reading soon became $500, and then $1,500, to continue “the work.”

About three months into her relationship with Russell, Smith tentatively volunteered that her father had some money, and they came up with a plan to coax out some cash: Smith would tell her father that she was trying to improve her life, to get back on the right track. She would lie about needing help with tuition, therapy, and expensive sleep studies. Her family and friends had grown worried—Smith didn’t seem like herself—and her father agreed at first to help.

Smith had never lied to her father before, but Russell explained that if she didn’t do “the work,” then Smith’s father would get sick and die. And Smith loved her father, right? Smith nodded vigorously, the worst-case scenario never far from her mind. She felt lucky to have someone like Russell helping her.

Smith’s father started sending cash but was increasingly reluctant as Smith’s self-help bills mounted. Emboldened, Russell instructed Smith to tell her father that she needed $500,000 for a cutting-edge therapy that would erase her memories of an early-life trauma. Smith even sent her father a treatment plan she had assembled. Smith’s father demanded to speak with the therapist, so Russell had a relative play the part in a call that lasted more than an hour. Smith was also on the line, and when Russell didn’t think she sounded sufficiently distraught, Russell kicked her hard under the table to make her cry.

BY 2011, TWO years into their relationship, it was hard for Smith to keep up with the demands and expense of Russell’s spiritual program, despite the money she was taking from her father. Smith was now working on the soap opera One Life to Live. Crediting Russell with helping her land the gig, she handed over almost her entire paycheck. Smith had grown emotionally dependent on Russell; she had mostly stopped hanging out with her friends and kept her coworkers at arm’s length with a hollow smile. But Smith’s relationship with Russell was becoming increasingly fraught. At first, it had felt like Russell wanted to help her, that they were solving a problem together. But now, Russell was pushier and more explicit about all the terrible things that might happen to Smith and the people she loved if she didn’t unquestioningly cooperate.

As part of “the work,” Smith was told she had to clean Russell’s home and babysit her kids. Smith soon morphed into Russell’s personal assistant—booking vacations, arranging transportation, and running endless errands. She might be sent suddenly in the middle of the night to buy a TV or air conditioner, carrying the appliance on her back up the stairs to Russell’s apartment. Smith claimed Russell’s addiction to painkillers, muscle relaxers, and antianxiety meds inspired her to dispatch Smith to the city’s emergency rooms with a slew of made-up ailments—one time even telling her to pretend she’d been in a car accident—in order to get their hands on prescriptions.

Russell was surrounded by what seemed like a tight-knit extended family. In addition to her own parents and siblings, there was her common-law husband, Robert; Robert’s brothers, Tony John and Corry Blue; and the brothers’ parents, Archie and Candy. By Smith’s account, the dynamic was far from wholesome: There were fistfights, destroyed TVs, thrown furniture, and smashed bottles. Smith claims she saw Russell’s mother use a Taser on Russell’s sister. Over time, the violence was turned on Smith if she questioned or disobeyed instructions. Russell would insist that the “devil” was in Smith and that she had to be “cleansed” through beatings. One time, Smith says she was forced naked into a freezing-cold bathtub while Russell lit various objects and then shook and hit her as if it were an exorcism.

By this point, Russell had made two predictions that had (sort of) come true, and Smith was convinced of her psychic powers. Russell said that Smith’s father would have her incarcerated—a foretelling that was fulfilled when Smith went home and her father had her committed on a 72-hour psychiatric hold. When Smith was released from the hospital, she fled back to Russell, shaken by the prophecy.

In the midst of all of this, Smith found work in the wardrobe department of the TV series Madam Secretary. It was a dream job, but working full-time and often staying up until the middle of the night to meet Russell’s demands, Smith developed sleep-deprived vertigo. She was also drowning in debt. Smith says that Russell told her to rack up charges on her credit cards and even had Smith sign leases and rental agreements on the family’s behalf. She was told to buy a Bentley and pay for an apartment in Marina del Rey, California. The family took trips to Hawaii, Las Vegas, and Austin, attending Formula One races and a Stevie Wonder concert. Unable to keep up with payments, Smith saw her credit destroyed. But the family kept spending. Smith says Russell developed a taste for Louis Vuitton handbags and bought herself a $150,000 diamond ring. Her family posted their vacations on social media while Smith was back at home, paying for all of it.

All the anxiety of Smith’s early years in the city, when she was trying to gain a foothold in life professionally and personally, had been supplanted by the relatively straightforward but almost impossible aim of keeping one psychic satisfied. Smith was constantly doing cleanup on her relationship with Russell and her family. Russell’s mother and brother-in-law stole keys to Smith’s apartment, ensuring she had nowhere to hide. Smith says that, once, trying to track her down, they showed up and threatened Smith’s neighbor. It wasn’t just terrifying; it was embarrassing.

Smith soon realized it was futile to try to have any kind of life beyond Russell’s needs. She quit her job, despite feeling trapped between desperately wanting out of the relationship, shame at handing over so much control and stealing from her father, and terror at what might happen if she tried to leave.

BY 2013, SMITH’S father had forked over more than $1 million. His relationship with his daughter badly frayed, he was disappointed and done. But Russell told Smith “the work” still wasn’t finished. Smith had quit her job, so Russell came up with a new way for her to make money.

“Sex sells,” Russell told Smith, as if it were a demand of the universe and out of her hands. Russell instructed Smith to pack a suitcase and sent her to Washington, D.C., where she didn’t know anyone. She was instructed to start listing ads for sensual massage services—and the suggestion of more—on websites like Backpage.com. Soon, Smith was moving from hotel room to hotel room, seeing as many as 17 clients a day. Russell had become even more caustic and demanding, now frequently threatening violence. Smith claims that one night, Russell told her that if she didn’t come up with $10,000 quickly, Russell would infect her with HIV. Smith, estranged from her family and penniless, believed her. She hustled to make the payment.

Smith was in a perpetual state of fear. Her body was broken and didn’t even feel like hers anymore, and she was still chronically sleep deprived, with Russell and her family tag-teaming with nearly 24-hour demands. Soon, Russell told Smith that the money she was bringing in from “massage services” still wasn’t enough to keep the demons at bay. She would have to work harder, finagling jewelry and other expensive goods from her clients. She instructed Smith to tell them that she was in debt to people who wanted to hurt her. She should give her clients an opportunity to save her. Russell cracked open a window into her own grooming techniques, the manipulation tactics that had been passed down in her own family like a silver tea set.

After successfully conning a few men for extra cash, Smith met Daniel Zancan. He was married and had two kids and was the chief financial officer of his wife’s family business. Zancan, 34, with glasses and short brown hair, was, like Smith, relatively sheltered. He had graduated from a private high school, went to a good college, earned his accounting license, and made six figures. But despite his circumstances, he was looking for more—which led him to the racy ads on Backpage.com.

Zancan quickly became one of Smith’s regulars and, despite himself, fell in love. To him, Smith was wounded and delicate, someone who needed taking care of. To Russell, Zancan was another gullible mark, someone whose dissatisfaction could be easily exploited. She told Smith that her powers “saw money” around Zancan.

Smith was ordered to sell Zancan a tragic fictional narrative: that she had been abused by her father, who was now suing her. The court costs were bleeding her dry, and she had borrowed money from the wrong people—dangerous people, loan sharks. They wanted it back and sometimes held her against her will for days at a time, assaulting her. They threatened to do even worse.

Zancan jumped at the chance to be her knight in shining armor. But he had to be careful. He didn’t have a lot of money, and he couldn’t tip off his wife or in-laws. He started funneling small amounts to Smith—$2,000 here, $2,500 there. But in January 2017, Smith told him that she needed a lot more—$100,000. Russell had Smith tell Zancan that because she didn’t have the money, she could pay off the debt with a pair of expensive Rolex watches instead. Smith and Zancan made their way to a high-end jewelry store in northern Virginia, where Zancan filled out a credit application for a $10,000 line of credit—which wasn’t enough to buy even one of the watches.

Smith’s phone buzzed with texts from Russell’s family posing as the angry loan sharks, and Zancan was terrified about what the men might do to her. (Some of the calls and texts were coming from Florida, where Russell and her family were vacationing. Smith had booked their trip.) In a state of desperation, an idea was floated: What if he tapped into his employer’s ample resources? As the CFO, he had access to their bank accounts.

On January 11, 2017, Zancan embezzled $110,000 via a wire transfer he sent to Smith’s personal account. The next day, Smith converted the stolen funds into a cashier’s check, which she took to a check-cashing place in New York. Russell texted Smith to stay calm as she presented the large sum to the teller. “Don’t panic this is negativity it’s the devil trying to attack you and we will not except [sic] it rebuke it in the name of Jesus your powers are coming through,” dictated Russell. When the check was successfully cashed, Smith dutifully handed over every cent.

Privately, Smith was fighting her instincts. But she knew better than to cross Russell. On more than one occasion, Smith says she tried to walk out of Russell’s apartment, only to have Russell grab her by the hair and drag her back in, leaving bruises and threatening to kill her. Once, Russell issued a vague threat that her own young son would be harmed if Smith left. So Smith stuck with the plan, Russell telling her it would take just a little more money, that they were doing all of this to help Smith, and that things would get better.

THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN Smith and Russell, while dysfunctional and violent, was also strikingly affectionate. The now-yearslong spell was an incredibly potent mixture of fear and dependence. Smith didn’t just take Russell’s instructions; she clung to the tiniest morsels of care and actively sought Russell’s counsel. She spoke fondly of her to Zancan and other clients, telling them that the only bright spot in her life was her good friend, Gina. Isolated and unable to articulate how powerful Russell had become, she was intent on preserving a bond that seemed essential. The two were completely enmeshed, Smith doing Russell’s bidding for scraps of approval. It had to feel a bit like love when nothing else in Smith’s life did.

But Russell was firmly in control. Smith says that when it came to Zancan, Russell was clear: “Make sure he loves you enough that he would do anything for you.” Russell and her extended family continued spending lavishly, buying Louis Vuitton luggage, Tiffany and Cartier jewelry, and Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet watches. Smith was forced to turn up the pressure on Zancan, telling him she needed $500,000 in cash.

One night, while Zancan was driving home from work, Smith called and said a loan shark named “Tony” (impersonated by Gina’s brother-in-law, Tony John) wanted to speak with him. Hammering home the threat, he said he knew where Zancan lived and worked. “Do I need to tell you where your kids go to school?” asked “Tony.” Zancan, panicking, agreed to steal the money and make the payment. Later, when he was en route to deliver the cash, one of Robert’s brothers took a picture of his license plate while he was in transit, which the family had Smith text to him. They wanted him to know that he was being watched.

Inspired by their new tactic, Russell and her family created additional characters to shake down Zancan. “Sammie” and “Santino” were even more sadistic; they gleefully told Zancan that they planned to beat Smith up—and worse. Zancan was breaking under the pressure. On February 5, 2017, Smith texted Russell in the middle of the night to tell her that Zancan was sobbing in their hotel room. “Tell him not to cry tell him that you love him very much,” Russell texted back. A few doors away, in their own room at the same hotel, Russell and Robert were taking videos of their young daughter posing with fat stacks of Zancan’s cash.

Later, Russell texted Smith to ask how Zancan was doing. Better, responded Smith. “We did good,” texted Smith. “Love you.” Russell texted back three crying-laughing emojis. “Love you,” she added. Russell then told Smith to delete her messages and get a burner phone. Shortly after, Tony John, impersonating a mobster in a call with Smith and Zancan, convinced Zancan to produce $1.6 million in gold bars.

Zancan was terrified but committed to a future with Smith. They would get through this mess and live happily ever after. On February 27, 2017, Smith texted Russell a picture. It was her left hand, her ring finger now heavy with a massive diamond engagement ring. Russell asked how many carats it was, and Smith guessed two, including the diamond-studded band. “Remember don’t fall in love and get too emotionally attached he only is doing this because you are emotionally supporting him,” texted Russell. Smith promised she was only “playing the part,” that she knew the difference between real and fake love.

Zancan had put aside $80,000 in gold bars that he hoped to use to start a new life with Smith. But soon after he put it in his car, Smith called to tell him a turf war had broken out between the gangsters. Santino had shot Tony. Santino wanted another $50,000 or Smith wouldn’t be allowed to leave. He threatened to rape her. Zancan liquidated the gold bars and handed $50,000 over to Smith at a Starbucks near Times Square. She gave it to Russell. Zancan and Smith drove to a hotel in Baltimore to spend the night, but not long after they checked in, the family started texting with more demands.

Zancan couldn’t take it anymore. He left Baltimore and started driving toward Texas. He was planning on collecting fake IDs there that he and Smith could use to escape for good. But when Zancan didn’t show up for work, his colleagues started digging around in his records and discovered the missing money. On April 6, 2017, Zancan was arrested. He had stolen more than $4 million, and he told the FBI everything. In a letter to the court, his parents suggested that Zancan’s vulnerability was being unusually trusting. “It is a good quality until it isn’t,” they wrote.

The FBI wanted to interview Russell and Smith, and Russell’s family hustled to come up with a cover story. They also decided that Russell, now 28, and Smith would get married, creating spousal privilege and ensuring that Smith couldn’t be compelled to testify against Russell. Smith was told to get burner phones to create “fake” conversations with Russell, crafting the impression that they were in love. They married at City Hall in New York.

But that wasn’t enough. According to Russell’s defense team, Robert’s mother, Candy, coerced Smith and her daughter-in-law to sign a notarized confession implicating themselves and absolving herself, her husband, and her sons of any illegal acts. Before Smith, now 32, went to her FBI interview in late April, the family threatened that she would spend the rest of her life in prison if she didn’t do exactly what she was told. Candy handed her two Valiums and told her it would help her “appear relaxed” during the interrogation. The Evans family (Robert’s brother) also made Smith sign a notarized confession and film a statement that absolved Russell and her family of any responsibility. But it wasn’t enough to assuage the family’s concerns that Smith might turn on them or that Zancan might successfully implicate them.

ON OCTOBER 19, 2017, a federal grand jury returned an indictment against Smith; she was arrested six days later. After eight years of terror, Smith felt a wave of relief as she was taken into custody. She was assigned to a maximum-security section of the D.C. Jail, where she bunked with a convicted murderer, and her stress-related chronic cough almost immediately ceased.

With so many details to disentangle, it would take another six months for a grand jury to return a 13-count indictment of fraud and extortion charges against Russell and her family. Russell and Robert split up, and the unified front fractured. Robert, his brothers, and his parents pleaded guilty to a litany of charges (Robert Evans and his brother Tony John Evans pleaded guilty to interference with interstate commerce by extortion; Corry Blue Evans pleaded guilty to bank fraud; Archie Kaslov pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud; Candy Evans pleaded guilty to tampering with a witness by corrupt persuasion or misleading conduct) and accepted sentences that ranged from one to five years.”

Russell eventually agreed to plead guilty to one count of interference with interstate commerce by extortion. She convinced prosecutors to propose a limited prison sentence, in light of her dramatic upbringing and her promise to stay out of trouble. She received permission to live in Los Angeles, supposedly to help an ailing family member. But in 2024, Russell was arrested in connection to the young musician’s case. Prosecutors immediately recognized a pattern in the musician’s account: promising spiritual healing for steep fees, encouraging the theft of almost $200,000 from the musician’s wealthy father, and eventually driving her into sex work before her instincts had a chance to catch up. Russell’s L.A. arrest violated the conditions of her relatively lax sentencing deal, and it was revoked by the court. On July 18, 2024, she was sentenced to more than 10 years and five months in prison, which she is presently serving in Oklahoma. She was also ordered to pay $4,217,542.86 in restitution.

As Russell’s court battle played out, Smith was able to convince prosecutors that while she’d participated in extortion schemes, she’d also been a victim who had handed all her money and power to a woman who had threatened and exploited her. (The marriage between the pair was annulled in 2019.)

On September 9, 2024, Smith pleaded to one count of conspiracy to commit bank and wire fraud and was sentenced to time served and 36 months of supervised release. “Coercion is a complex thing,” noted Judge Tanya S. Chutkan, at Smith’s sentencing. “But what I have learned…is that under the right combination of stress, pressure, and psychological circumstances, seemingly normal people will do very abnormal things.”

Since her release from Russell’s grip, Smith has become an anti-trafficking advocate and now works for 3Strands, an organization dedicated to combating trafficking through education and reintegration programs. Last year, Smith provided testimony to a congressional task force in support of The Trafficking Survivors Relief Act, which was passed into law in January 2026 and allows victims of sex trafficking to have their arrest/conviction records vacated and expunged—Smith seems to have availed herself of this law as her criminal history is no longer publicly available. (The court records in her case were accessed and saved for this article before public access was removed.) Smith declined to comment for this article; instead, the above is based on the voluminous court records filed by both prosecutors and defendants in the Russell, Smith, and Zancan prosecutions.

In January 2026, Smith was pardoned by President Donald Trump.

It’s also worth noting that though Smith identifies as a victim of human trafficking, none of the people involved in her odyssey were charged or convicted of human or sex trafficking.

“There is no black and white survivor story,” she wrote in her testimony, alluding to the various definitions—both legal and informal—of the word. “There are all types of trafficking in this world.... I am determined to use my lived experience from these horrific years to bring meaningful change and protect others.”

The declines reversed Wednesday's rally, when bitcoin climbed back above $80,000 following the U.S. midterm elections and signs that the Binance hack had not caused broader market disruption.

Midterm election results appeared to generate short-term optimism, but analysts say they haven't resolved macroeconomic uncertainties.

As of 2 p.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 were down about 3% for the day, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite had dropped 4.7%. The Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX, surged approximately 60%, reflecting heightened investor anxiety.

It should be noted that liquidation figures are typically based on publicly available data, which may significantly understate the extent of market liquidations.

The reversal suggests Wednesday's rebound may have been driven more by temporary optimism than a meaningful improvement in the market's underlying conditions, according to Wintermute.

However, those factors proved short-lived as broader macroeconomic pressures persisted.

"It's probably a combination of all of them in some way. What matters is that all of them seemed to be so short-lived that it actually didn't really matter," said Jasper De Maere, an OTC trader at Wintermute. "Trump is still the president for two years, the Middle East is still escalating, inflation is elevated into a strong U.S. economy."

Beyond the immediate market pressures, the election results may also complicate the outlook for crypto regulation, potentially tempering some of the optimism that helped drive Wednesday's rebound.

Paul Howard, senior director at Wincent, said the Democrats' strengthened position in Congress could make bipartisan cooperation necessary for meaningful progress on crypto legislation over the next two years. With the Clarity Act's prospects uncertain, Howard expects the existing regulatory framework to largely remain intact until the next election cycle.

Ryan Kirkley, CEO of Global Settlement Network, said the election could delay crypto legislation but wouldn't fundamentally change longer-term institutional demand for digital assets.

"Investors are still focused on liquidity, interest rates and the broader economy, and those factors will continue to influence the market regardless of which party controls Congress," Kirkley said.

If the weakness continues, Wintermute identified $73,000 and $68,000 as the next levels to watch for bitcoin. The firm said it would need to see bitcoin convincingly reclaim and hold $80,000 before turning more positive.

#5126. US Voters Back AI Data Center Restrictions in At Least 29 Communities

US Voters Back AI Data Center Restrictions in At Least 29 Communities

Voters in at least 29 U.S. jurisdictions backed bans or restrictions on data-center development Tuesday, according to The Washington Post, dealing a new setback to the massive infrastructure buildout behind artificial intelligence.

The measures ranged from outright prohibitions to requirements for additional public approval. Some were nonbinding advisory votes, meaning their passage does not automatically stop construction.

Ballotpedia tracked 41 data-center measures on November 3 ballots across 10 states. Twenty-eight were framed so that a yes vote would curb development, while 13 would permit or support projects, meaning rejecting one of the latter could also count as a defeat for developers.

Ohio produced some of the clearest results. All 10 charter measures backed by the grassroots group Conserve Ohio passed, according to the Post, and more than three-quarters of voters in Hubbard, Ohio, supported a ban on data centers.

The negative sentiment is so big that voters in Granville, Trenton, and Sunbury backed restrictions with margins of roughly 78% to 82%.

In Illinois, nearly 80% of voters in Joliet Township rejected an advisory proposal supporting AI data centers. In Janesville, Wisconsin, more than 60% approved a requirement for another public vote before major development at a former General Motors site linked to a proposed data center.

These facilities house the chips and servers used to train and run AI systems. Their appetite for electricity has turned proposed campuses into local fights over utility bills and grid capacity, while opponents also raise concerns about water use, noise and deals struck without public scrutiny.

AI companies are aware of the growing backlash and are already working to counter it. Some are stepping up lobbying efforts, while others are turning to public relations campaigns to reshape public perception. OpenAI, for instance, has sought to rebrand data centers as “compute campuses,” in an effort to distance the facilities from the negative connotations increasingly associated with them.

The votes arrived alongside victories by politicians promising tougher oversight of data centers. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas after campaigning for a moratorium on new projects, while Ohio's governor-elect Amy Acton also supports a pause and stricter rules.

Industry leaders have warned that blanket restrictions would put U.S. AI investment at risk. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink said last month that a broad moratorium could have serious economic consequences. "If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession," he said.

#5121. US Bank Regulator Issues First AI Framework as Banks Battle Rogue Agents

US Bank Regulator Issues First AI Framework as Banks Battle Rogue Agents

The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued its first supervisory framework for artificial intelligence in banking today, telling examiners to focus less on how powerful an AI system is and more on what happens when it makes a mistake.

The OCC's framework addresses that very concern, although the regulator has not linked its issuance to those specific incidents.

In a section covering operational resilience, the agency warns that external agents operated by customers, fintechs, or other businesses could create risks for banks even when the banks don't control those systems.

It suggests examiners consider measures including identity verification, delegated permissions, transaction limits, monitoring, and the ability to suspend or revoke access.

The guidelines aim to tackle the dilemma of how to let customers use AI assistants to manage their finances without giving autonomous software unrestricted access to accounts that banks are already facing.

The new OCC guidance arrives less than two weeks after reports that major banks were discovering unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, sometimes taking actions that appeared to go beyond users' instructions.

Morgan Stanley was blocking outside agents, while JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi were restricting access, according to an Axios report on October 22. Bank executives described the situation as "horrifying," raising questions about who controls an autonomous agent once it has access to someone's money.

The OCC's framework makes a distinction between an AI system's technical sophistication and the damage it could cause.

A simple agent authorized to initiate financial transactions may present greater risk than a more advanced model limited to writing internal documents, the regulator said.

Under the 22-page framework, examiners can consider the consequences of failure, whether an action can be reversed, and how much control humans retain over the system.

The agency outlines four illustrative risk tiers. Fully autonomous payment agents and real-time credit decision systems fall into the highest category, while basic internal productivity tools occupy the lowest.

Higher-risk systems may warrant tighter restrictions on autonomy, independent testing, and human approval before consequential actions can proceed.

The framework also addresses AI systems that continue operating while making harmful decisions. Suggested safeguards include circuit breakers, rate limits, restricted permissions, and emergency shutdown controls.

Those considerations are especially relevant to the outside agents described in Axios's earlier reporting, where banks struggled to distinguish legitimate customer-authorized software from systems operating beyond their intended permissions.

The OCC stressed that the document does not create new regulatory requirements or enforceable standards for banks.

Instead, it gives examiners a way to evaluate AI within existing operational, compliance, and cybersecurity risk categories. Banks are not required to establish a separate AI risk category.

The document uses the mandatory term "Super Intelligence," which the Donald Trump administration insists on using in place of “artificial intelligence,” but its scope includes conventional AI and “autonomous agents” rather than only hypothetical systems with intelligence beyond human capabilities.

The framework covers AI used in payments, fraud detection, customer service, and other banking operations. It also extends its risk considerations to external AI agents connecting through bank channels.

The OCC said it intends to update the guidance as the technology develops. For now, its illustrative risk scale puts autonomous payment agents in the highest-risk category, regardless of how well they perform in testing.

#5119. What Is The Bare Minimum Amount Of Strength Training You Need To Do For It To Be Effective? Here's What Trainers Say

Right up there with a balanced diet, strength training is the OG biohack for longevity, and the key to a strong, healthy body. But whether you’re a beginner or seasoned athlete, that begs the question: How much strength training do you actually need to see results?

If you look to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for answers, they say that adults need at least two days of “muscle-strengthening activity" per week for their overall health. But, resistance training even once a week was enough to make progress for beginners, per a study in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation.

"While it may seem the small amount of volume would be insignificant, this study demonstrates that some exercise is better than no exercise,” says certified personal trainer Natalya Vasquez. But as your skill level progresses, you’ll need to increase the intensity and volume of your workouts to elicit more muscle growth.

Below, experts explain exactly how much strength training is enough based on your fitness level and goals.

Meet the experts: Tina Tang, CPT, is a certified personal trainer, strength coach, and founder of Iron Strong Fitness. Natalya Vasquez, CPT, is a certified personal trainer, health coach, and founder of On Your Terms Coaching.

The following cheat-sheet will give you an idea of how many days a week you should strength train.

While once a week was enough for the folks in the aforementioned study to make progress, they only looked at a single exercise: the leg press. Vasquez says that ideally, beginners looking to build total-body muscle and strength should start with two, or even three, nonconsecutive strength training sessions per week.

This frequency helps build a habit (key for those just starting out) and provides your body with the necessary stimulus for initial muscle growth, while also allowing for plenty of time to recover. But, your sessions don't have to be long: Initially, each session can be as short as 15 to 20 minutes, and you can gradually increase to 45- to 60-minute workouts as you build endurance, says certified personal trainer Tina Tang, CPT.

As for how you structure your workouts, Vasquez says you can either do two to three full-body workouts, or a three-day split, like a push/pull/legs workout, where your training is organized by muscle group.

For a full-body routine, Vasquez suggests completing one exercise per muscle group for three to five sets of five to eight reps per workout. For a three-day split, complete three to four exercises for the same muscle group for two to three sets of five to eight reps.

Vasquez likes the five to eight rep range because she says this helps develop functional hypertrophy: “We don’t just want to gain muscle, we want to have actual strength where this muscle growth is functional,” she says.

“You don’t need complicated gym equipment to get results,” says Vasquez. “Dumbbells and bands are affordable, convenient, and versatile options for exercising at home, and as your strength increases, gym access may be beneficial since it’ll give you additional equipment and a wider selection of weights.”

In this case, the trainers suggest strength training three times a week, and depending on the intensity and volume of the workout, each session should range between 30 to 60 minutes, Tang says. “This frequency is effective for preserving muscle mass and strength while ensuring adequate recovery and adaptation.”

However, overall volume may be more important that days per week, according to a 2021 review in Sports Medicine. The researchers conclude that it's possible to see gains by training anywhere from one to four days per week so long as you're getting in at least four sets of six to 15 reps per muscle group per week.

The key here will be to follow the principle of progressive overload. Gradually increasing the weight, sets and or reps, over time will continually challenge the muscles, stimulate growth, and improve bone density, says Tang. “The body craves movement, and once it's accustomed to a certain level of activity, it needs more of a challenge to keep making gains."

Good news: The longer you’ve been strength training, the less work you’ll need to maintain your gains since your muscles are composed of more fibers, says Vasquez. “So if you’ve been strength training five times per week for a decade and then something happens in your life that doesn’t allow you to work out as much, you’ll still be able to maintain your muscle with one full-body workout per week,” she says. However, this would be the bare minimum, and resistance training two to three times a week is still the ideal sweet spot.

In terms of the type of training, Tang also recommends full-body workouts to maintain balanced muscle development and overall strength. Look to hit all the major movement patterns for best results. For each exercise, Vasquez says to aim to complete three to five sets of five to eight reps.

Aside from logging miles, strength training at least twice a week is a crucial part of every running regimen, says Tang. “Ideally, one session can focus on bilateral, foundational movements, while a second session allows for a more specialized approach, targeting unilateral exercises, core stability, and hip strength,” she explains. “This balance ensures you're not only building overall strength but also addressing the specific needs that support running performance and injury prevention.”

Indeed, the addition of two to four strength training sessions a week helped mid- to long-distance runners prevent injury and run faster, according to a 2024 meta-analysis in the journal Sports Medicine.

Workouts should range between 30 to 60 minutes and rep ranges can vary from five to eight (with heavier weight and for more advanced strength trainers) to 12 to 20 reps (for runners newer to strength training and using lighter weights), Vasquez says.

FWIW, the meta-analysis notes that plyometric training and "high load" strength training (using weights at 80% of your one rep max or heavier), specifically, improved running economy.

For this goal, Tang says to strength train at least twice a week. Doing so "helps build and maintain muscle mass and bone density, which is crucial for protecting bones and joints as we age, and this frequency provides a balance between stimulating the muscles and allowing for adequate recovery,” she says.

Plus, regular resistance training helps strengthen tendons and ligaments, in turn, supporting joint stability and overall musculoskeletal health, she adds.

Full-body workouts and compound exercises like deadlifts, overhead presses, and squats are ideal since they involve multiple joints and mimic how your body moves in real life, says Vasquez. Depending on your experience, this could look like choosing two to three exercises and doing three to five sets for five to eight reps (to focus on building functional strength) per workout.

No matter your goals, strength training is certainly worth your time. Aside from supporting your overall wellbeing, picking up weights can prevent injury, improve metabolic health, reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, and support bone density, especially in women, says Vasquez.

In fact, approximately one in five women over age 50 have osteoporosis (a condition that causes bones to become weak and brittle), but strength training can help enhance bone density and reduce the risk of fractures, says Tang.

Sarcopenia, an age-related progressive loss of muscle mass strength, is another common condition among women, and after age 30, you can gradually begin losing muscle mass each decade. Fortunately, strength training can again help combat the effects and reverse muscle loss, says Tang.

Finally, regular weight training supports balance, mobility, and functional strength which are crucial for performing daily activities and living independently, Tang says. “Strength training acts as an investment in our future health, ensuring that we maintain physical strength and resilience for the long term.”

Andi Breitowich is a freelance writer who covers health, fitness, relationships, beauty, and smart living. She is a graduate of Emory University and Northwestern University's Medill School of Journalism. Her work has appeared in Women's Health, POPSUGAR, Food & Wine, What To Expect, Cosmopolitan, Men's Health, and elsewhere. As a former collegiate pole vaulter, she loves all things fitness and has yet to meet a group workout class she doesn't like.
