#5116. Walking This Many Steps a Day Could Help Lower Your Risk of Alzheimers—It’s Less Than You Think

You've probably heard by now that exercising regularly is good for your brain and may even help lower your risk of Alzheimer's disease. But new research suggests that you don't have to kill yourself at the gym to harness these perks.

The study, which was published in Nature Medicine last year but is making the rounds now, found that taking just 3,000 steps a day is linked to significantly lower rates of cognitive decline, along with fewer markers of Alzheimer's disease.

It's worth pointing out that 3,000 steps isn't a ton (we're talking about walking about 1.5 miles in a day). That makes this a very doable goal to aim for. But how accurate is this, and what does it suggest about the 10,000-step goal everyone throws around? Doctors weigh in.

Meet the experts: Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center; Nikhil Satchidanand, PhD, a research assistant professor of medicine in the Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences at the University at Buffalo; Liron Sinvani, MD, director of research and innovation for the Institute for Healthy Aging at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research; Anna Hohler, MD, regional director of Neurology for Westchester, Northwell Health, and chair of Neurology for Northern Westchester and Phelps hospitals; and Shannel Elhelou, PsyD, a neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, California.

For the observational study, researchers analyzed data from 296 people between the ages of 50 and 90 who participated in the Harvard Aging Brain Study, a long-running study that tracks brain changes in older adults. None of the participants had dementia or signs of cognitive decline at the start of the study.

Participants wore waistband pedometers to track their physical activity and underwent PET brain scans to measure the amount of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles (both are hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease). Participants also underwent cognitive assessment about 9.3 years later.

The researchers found that people who had higher step counts also had lower rates of cognitive decline. Higher step counts were also linked with a slower buildup of tau. Not only that, but walking 3,000 to 5,000 steps daily seemed to slow progression of Alzheimer's disease in people who were at a higher risk of developing it.

Specifically, those considered high risk for Alzheimer's disease who walked 3,000 to 5,000 steps a day had a three-year delay in developing cognitive decline. People who walked 5,000 to 7,500 steps daily saw a seven-year delay in their cognitive decline.

Those who were more sedentary saw a buildup of tau proteins in the brain, along with faster rates of decline in their cognition and daily functioning.

There are probably a few things behind this, according to neurologists. A big one is that physical activity is simply good for the brain. "It improves blood flow, supports cardiovascular and metabolic health, reduces systemic inflammation, and may help protect brain cells from aging-related damage," says Nikhil Satchidanand, PhD, research assistant professor of medicine in the Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences at the University at Buffalo.

Working out also helps stimulate the release of protective molecules like irisin and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which support the health and connectivity of brain cells, says Liron Sinvani, MD, director of research and innovation for the Institute for Healthy Aging at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research. "Exercise also improves cardiovascular fitness, and what is good for the heart is good for the brain," she adds. Daily walks can support your cardiovascular system and may lower the risk of vascular or multi-infarct dementia, according to Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center.

Neurologists applaud how approachable the findings are. "Importantly, 3,000 steps is an achievable goal for many people, making regular physical activity more sustainable over time," says Anna Hohler, MD, regional director of Neurology for Westchester, Northwell Health, and chair of Neurology for Northern Westchester and Phelps hospitals. "Consistent movement, even at lower levels, appears to contribute to better cognitive resilience and may help reduce the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease."

But Dr. Satchidanand says that "there's nothing magical" about 3,000 steps. "The brain doesn't suddenly start benefiting from physical activity when someone reaches a particular number of daily steps," he says. "The relationship between physical activity and health exists along a continuum."

Step count also only reveals one dimension of a person's physical activity, Dr. Satchidanand says. "They don't tell us much about walking intensity, cardiovascular fitness, strength training, or other forms of movement that may also influence brain health," he says.

Dr. Satchidanand says it's also important to consider that people who develop Alzheimer's disease may move less, which could also influence findings. "Early Alzheimer's-related changes in the brain could themselves lead people to become less physically active, even before noticeable cognitive symptoms develop," he points out.

The idea that you only need to log 3,000 steps a day to slow down cognitive decline is definitely appealing—and far less than the 10,000-step milestone that gets thrown around a lot. So where does that magical 10,000 standard come from?

Turns out, it’s actually an arbitrary number from a marketing campaign for a Japanese step counter. Since then, research has actually suggested that 10,000 steps is more than most people need to be healthy. So, if you want to walk that many steps a day, more power to you—but just know you don’t actually need to walk that far to reap health benefits.

Movement in general benefits the brain, so it’s hard to go wrong if you find something you love.

"My advice is to find activities you enjoy and can realistically sustain," says Shannel Elhelou, PsyD, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, California. "Consistency matters, and an achievable routine can grow over time."

This can include brisk walking, swimming, dancing, or cycling, depending on your abilities and preferences, Elhelou says. "I also encourage people to consider what makes movement meaningful to them," she continues.

Dr. Satchidanand also notes that people shouldn't feel boxed in by a specific step count. "Moving more, particularly among people who are currently inactive, is beneficial for overall health and may help support healthier brain aging," he says.

#5114. Why Am I Always So Tired? 15 Reasons You May Have Fatigue

Allergies, stress, and sugar could all play a part in your energy levels.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The most relatable statement of all time: “I’m exhausted.” Life is stressful, busy, and often feels like an impossible balancing act. Beyond the demands of endless work tasks and social obligations, legit health reasons could explain lingering fatigue. If you’re chugging coffee on the regular and still wondering, Why am I so tired? it's worth considering whether something in your body is causing your low energy.

Obviously, if you stay up binging a new series or push yourself harder than usual while training for an upcoming race, you’re gonna feel sluggish the next day. But there’s a difference between feeling tapped out sometimes and long bouts of fatigue that won’t go away.

Meet the experts: Antoinette LaDawn Price, MD, MPH, is a family medicine doctor at Emory Physician Group Practice; Purvi Parikh, MD, is an allergist and immunologist with Allergy & Asthma Network; Sobia Khan, MD, is the director of Women's Center for Comprehensive Care at Baylor College of Medicine; Jessica Cording, RD, is the author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; Monifa Seawell, MD, is a board-certified psychiatrist in Atlanta, Georgia

“Fatigue is chronic extreme tiredness,” says Antoinette LaDawn Price, MD, MPH, at Emory Physician Group Practice. Fatigue can show up as headaches, dizziness, and achy and sore muscles, irritability, brain fog, and moodiness; it manifests differently in each person.

If you always feel drained, it may be time for you to consult your doctor about your symptoms. If you feel like something is off, don’t ignore it—there are many health issues, both mental and physical, that can make it difficult for you to last through the entire day without wanting to collapse in bed. Here are possible causes of fatigue, according to doctors.

Classic symptoms of seasonal allergies include sneezing and having watery eyes. Less common symptoms include low energy and fatigue. “If left untreated, seasonal allergies can cause fatigue,” says Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with Allergy & Asthma Network. Why? Your body works hard to fend off the allergen, and that takes extra energy. That’s true whether you're allergic to outdoor triggers like ragweed or pollen, or to indoor allergens like dust mites, Dr. Parikh says.

Allergens aren’t the only things that can trigger fatigue—allergy medications can, too. “Some of the over-the-counter allergy pills like antihistamines unfortunately cause fatigue as well,” says Dr. Parikh.

How to fix it: If allergies leave you feeling completely spent, your current treatment plan may not be working. So, check in with your doctor about your options. They’ll likely recommend medication (or a different one) to help get things under control. Running a HEPA air purifier at home can also help clear the air, notes Dr. Parikh.

While going hard during your at-home workouts can wear you out, the opposite can do the same. “The human body gets more tired with progressive sedentary habits due to generalized reconditioning of the body and, ultimately, muscle loss,” explains Sobia Khan, MD, an assistant professor of general internal medicine and the director of Women's Center for Comprehensive Care at Baylor College of Medicine.

Basically, your body takes a “use it or lose it” approach to fitness. If you don’t exercise regularly, you’ll feel more tired when you start moving and even when you’re at rest.

How to fix it: This solution is pretty simple—get moving more. Just a reminder, the general physical activity recommendation is 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise each week, plus muscle-strengthening activity at least two days a week. Once you start moving again, it’ll be easier to get through your day-to-day stuff without being a zombie.

When you eat sugary foods or foods high in refined carbs (think: white bread, pasta, pastries), your blood sugar spikes, according to Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. In the moment, that can make you feel kinda hyper. But unfortunately, you're also in for an inevitable crash, which can leave you feeling totally wiped.

If you keep overloading on sugar and refined carbs, you may also develop insulin resistance, Dr. Khan adds. That is when your body can’t use glucose (a.k.a. sugar) as well as it should for energy.

How to fix it: Cording says to cut back on sugar and refined carbs regularly. FWIW, the CDC recommends limiting added sugar to less than 10 percent of your total daily calories. (So, if you eat a 2,000-calorie diet, no more than 200 of those calories should come from added sugars.)

When you’re having sugary or carb-heavy foods, balance the meal with protein and fat, like adding nut butter to your crackers. This can help lower the odds that you’ll crash afterward, Cording says.

Stress isn’t just mental—it can affect you physically, too. “Your mind and body are closely linked and are in constant communication with one another,” says Monifa Seawell, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist in Atlanta, Georgia. “When there is a shift in your emotional state, be it positive or negative, it is not at all uncommon for that change to also show up in some physical way in your body.”

You can start getting headaches, an upset stomach, and, yep, fatigue, Dr. Seawell says.

How to fix it: The best approach is to address the root of your stress. While some stressors are unavoidable, doing your utmost to limit the ones you can address can be helpful.

Dr. Seawell also recommends scheduling 20 to 30 minutes of exercise each day. She says this can often boost your energy levels when you can’t completely eliminate your stress. If you’re still struggling, try talking to a licensed mental health professional. They “can help you process your emotions and learn healthy coping skills,” Dr. Seawell says.

Adults should be getting seven hours or more a night, according to the CDC. Definitely getting less? Enter: Fatigue.

“Minimum seven hours of sleep is required for effective rejuvenation of the body and restfulness of the brain,” says Dr. Khan. Here’s the thing: Even one night of bad sleep can mess with your circadian rhythm (your sleep-wake cycle) and throw you off for a few days, she says.

How to fix it: At baseline, the solution is simply to get more sleep. But sometimes that’s easier said than done. You need to first figure out what the culprit is—stress? Netflix? Crappy sleep hygiene?—and then address it. If that still doesn't work, talk to your doctor about your options. You may need an intervention such as cognitive behavioral therapy to treat insomnia, for example.

Depression can cause a range of symptoms, and decreased energy or fatigue is definitely one of them, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). “Whenever I am screening a patient for depression, feelings of fatigue and loss of energy are one of the symptoms I always inquire about,” says Dr. Seawell.

These are the symptoms of depression to be familiar with, according to the NIMH.

Worth noting: Not everyone with depression experiences every symptom, per the NIMH. So, it’s entirely possible for you to feel tired on the regular and not even realize that it’s due to depression.

How to fix it: In this case, you need to address the underlying cause of your fatigue before you’ll feel better. Depression can be treated with psychotherapy, medication, or a combination of the two. If you suspect that your fatigue is linked to depression, though, it’s best to talk to your doctor about getting evaluated.

Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck that produces hormones that regulate how your body uses energy. When it doesn't produce enough thyroid hormone, it causes a condition known as hypothyroidism, which can mess with or slow down many of your body's functions, according to MedlinePlus.

“Thyroid hormones have receptors on essentially every organ of the human body and their deficiency can cause fatigue by excessively slowing the metabolic pathways,” explains Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: The treatment for hypothyroidism is taking medication to replace the hormone that your own thyroid can no longer make or create a sufficient amount of to keep your body functioning normally. Just know this: It may take a little while to feel better. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication until you reach the optimal level.

Just because you’re on the mend from, say, a virus doesn’t mean you should expect to bounce back energy-wise automatically. Recovery can take time. "A viral or bacterial infection can cause dehydration, generalized inflammation, and immense fatigue," says Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: First, give yourself time to recoup. Drink plenty of water and just take it easy, and you should feel less tired and more like yourself in a week or two.

Anemia is a condition in which your blood has fewer than normal red blood cells or hemoglobin, according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI). Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that helps red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. According to the NHLBI, if you have anemia, your body doesn't get enough oxygen-rich blood. So, if you have the condition, you can struggle with “fatigue and excessive tiredness,” says Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: It depends on the type of anemia you have. For some types of mild to moderate anemia, you may just need to add OTC or prescription iron supplements to your regimen. But your doctor may also suggest certain vitamins, IV therapy, or medicines that make your body produce more red blood cells, according to the NHLBI. You may also need to incorporate more iron-rich foods into your diet. Basically, you should see your doc for this one.

Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. In some people, gluten damages the small intestine and causes symptoms like bloating, diarrhea, constipation, gas, nausea, stomach pain, vomiting, and yep, fatigue, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK). That happens to people with celiac disease.

This condition can also cause long-term digestive issues that keep you from getting the nutrients you need and, in turn, cause ongoing fatigue.

How to fix it: Celiac disease can be tricky to diagnose, but after a physical exam, your doctor may recommend a blood test and an intestinal biopsy to check for inflammation in your small intestine. If you are confirmed to have celiac disease, you’ll need to avoid foods containing gluten in the future.

This is a less likely diagnosis, but it’s still worth mentioning. MS is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the brain and spinal cord, damaging the myelin, the covering of nerve fibers, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS).

Fatigue is a very common symptom in people with MS—about 80 percent of patients struggle with it, according to the NMSS. The fatigue can significantly interfere with a person’s ability to function, even if they feel good otherwise. It can result from treatable medication side effects or other factors.

How to fix it: Specific treatments can help people with MS manage fatigue, including occupational therapy to simplify tasks at home, physical therapy to learn energy-saving ways to walk and do other day-to-day tasks, a regular exercise program, sleep regulation, and psychological interventions, per the NMSS.

This is another one to add to the category of “unlikely but worth knowing.” Cancer-related fatigue is incredibly common: At least 80 percent of people diagnosed with the condition experience it, according to the American Cancer Society (ACS). While cancer treatments could be to blame, people with cancer can also feel wiped out just from the disease itself. It can disrupt almost all metabolic pathways and sabotage the body's mitochondrial energy, Dr. Khan explains.

How to fix it: First, don't freak out that you have a serious health issue. But know that getting a proper diagnosis is important and, from there, proper treatment is needed, which usually involves chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, or immunotherapy. The exact course depends on what type of cancer you have and how advanced it is. That's why seeing your doctor to rule it out is key if you haven't been able to shake your tiredness for a long time.

Here's the thing: Our body needs a range of nutrients and a certain number of calories per day to run at its normal capacity. Those numbers vary for everyone. "You need to not only make sure that you're providing yourself with a sufficient amount of calories per day to function, but also you need to be providing yourself with the appropriate nutrients," says Dr. Price.

If you don't, which can add to the fatigue, Dr. Price adds, even the smallest task feels monumental. You can also become constipated, says Dr. Price, which can contribute to the fatigue.

How to fix it: Eating a well-balanced diet and making sure that you’re eating enough fruits, vegetables, and proteins s essential to combatting fatigue, says Dr. Price. With the right nutrients, your body can create the energy you need to go about your day.

You’ve heard it before, but it’s true: Caffeine is a drug. Once your body gets accustomed to it, especially if you have coffee or soda every day, you become dependent on it. While it gives you a boost, caffeine also comes with highs and lows, and that can make you feel extremely tired, says Dr. Price. “Because you're burning calories when you have caffeine, you're moving at a faster pace, and you get to your peak of exhaustion much quicker,” she explains.

If you absolutely need coffee to get through your day, that should be a warning sign. "You should not have to have coffee in order to function, and something else is going on in your life that is causing you to be extremely fatigued," notes Dr. Price.

How to fix it: Switch up how you get your caffeine and start weaning yourself off of it. It'll take some adjustment, and you might get headaches at first, but once your body no longer depends on coffee, you'll feel a lot better.

While the medical world is still trying to figure out the long-term effects of COVID-19, we do know the toll the disease has on your body is that it makes you extremely exhausted, says Dr. Price. Your body tries to recuperate when you're infected—you lose your appetite, your muscles are extremely fatigued, and your body works in overdrive.

“Your body is doing the most to get you back to your normal self and to fight off COVID, so once you're done with it, you're not just going to bounce right back to yourself," says Dr. Price. “It's also been shown that the peak symptoms of COVID can sometimes be 14 days later. People must keep in mind this isn't a short illness. There are different and great severities of it."

Long COVID usually occurs two months after a person had COVID, says Dr. Price. If, two months after contracting the novel coronavirus, you’re still feeling worn out, it could be long COVID, she says.

How to fix it: The best way to protect yourself against COVID and the long-term complications is to get vaccinated and boosted and keep practicing good hygiene. If you suspect you have long COVID, visit your primary care provider and discuss your symptoms, Dr. Price advises. They can help you figure out your next steps.

Feeling tired once in a while is pretty normal—but experiencing constant fatigue isn’t. If you’re struggling, Dr. Khan recommends seeing your doctor. They’ll likely order several tests, including a physical exam and blood work, to figure out what, if anything, is happening.

"It's never too soon to go and talk to your doctor," says Dr. Price. What you thought might be minor, the doctor might look into more. "Or maybe you started googling things and, of course, Google will tell you you're dying, so talking to your doctor can give you relief and reassurance," Dr. Price adds.

The upside: the sooner you seek help, the sooner you can get answers—and get back to your rejuvenated and energetic self.

UNLESS YOU'RE SHAVING with a top-notch wet or dry electric razor, you’ll need to first apply a product to prep the skin. There are really only two options: pre-shave oil and shaving cream. The truth is, your shave is only as good as the cream you use because the right shaving cream cushions the skin, reduces irritation, and locks in moisture for added comfort afterwards. It also helps the razor glide smoothly, preventing nicks and tugging.

Most importantly, it turns a tedious routine into a clean, refreshing experience. But not all shaving creams are created equal—some barely protect or soothe at all. To save your skin the abuse (and potential scars), I’ve rounded up the best options worth trying.

Jackfir The Classic checks every box I look for in a shaving cream. Its ingredients are clean, its scent soothing, and the formula protects the skin from irritation and cuts. Simply put, I got one of the closest, smoothest shaves I’ve ever had with this cream.

The creamy lather cushions the razor perfectly while aloe, cucumber, and panthenol keep the skin calm and hydrated. The scent is invigorating and woodsy, thanks to natural oils like cedarwood, vetiver, and chamomile instead of synthetic fragrances. This also makes it safe for sensitive skin without being entirely scentless.

On top of its long list of at least 70 percent organic ingredients, it even comes in sustainable packaging made from recycled materials. I generally shave with a safety razor for my face and a cartridge razor for my body (or when traveling), and Jackfir was perfect for both.

The razor you use isn’t solely responsible for shaving irritation. For many, simply switching to a gentler, more skin-friendly shaving cream will go a long way in preventing bumps and redness. You won’t find a better option than Harry’s Shave Cream, which is no surprise coming from what I dubbed the best skincare brand for clean-shaven men.

This cream packs powerful natural ingredients like eucalyptus oil, mint oil, and aloe vera, which work together to soothe skin and reduce irritation. It’s free of parabens, sulfates, or other common irritants, and its formula is equally thick and silky to protect and smooth skin. Best of all, it could double as the best value shaving cream at only $8 a container.

I’ve been cutting my own hair for over a decade, so I really only go to barbershops for one thing: a close and luxurious shave. But this shaving cream makes me wonder if I could eliminate those trips altogether. It’s the closest you’ll get to the barbershop experience with an incredible, soft lather that feels like a hot towel wrapped around your chin. Sure, it’s a little pricey and best applied with a brush—which I count as a positive—but it’s far less expensive and time-consuming than making a trip to your local shop.

If you’re prone to razor bumps and burning like me, this cream will feel like a godsend thanks to its rich and smooth lather that’s packed with ingredients that care for skin. The aloe vera and shea butter deliver deep hydration, keeping your face calm and protected while helping to prevent razor bumps and irritation.

The pair also works together to calm inflammation, moisturize, and create a protective barrier that helps prevent razor bumps and post-shave irritation. White tea extract then adds that clean, refreshing feel I always look for in a shaving cream. It’s soothing, nourishing, and bump-free.

I don’t use cartridge razors too often, as safety and electric razors tend to leave my sensitive skin less irritated. But if I’m traveling or in a hurry, I’ll turn to them—and rarely without this shave gel from GilletteLabs. The rapid foaming is as advertised, thickening in seconds for quick application.

It gives that fresh feeling once it hits your face before the razor even touches your skin. While it’s listed as having a cedar wood and orange peel scent, I rarely catch too much of it. But I prefer that, as I’d rather rely on my cologne for fragrance.

I implore you to use a shave oil in addition to a cream to minimize irritation as much as possible; however, if you really don’t have the time or desire to, use this. Atwater’s shaving cream is designed to pull double duty, preparing the skin before the razor touches it and protecting it throughout the shave. As a pre-shave, its blend of hydrating oils helps soften stubble and create a smooth, conditioned surface.

During shaving, ingredients like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil work together to cushion the blade, reduce friction, and keep the skin nourished. This combination leaves my skin feeling as calm and moisturized as it’ll get without using a pre-shave oil. Plus, it’s completely unscented, so it’s safe for even the most sensitive skin.

Dr. Squatch’s shave butter feels more like a creamy lotion than shaving cream, allowing the razor to glide smoothly across the skin while it also moisturizes. Together, they create a nourishing barrier that locks in moisture and helps reduce irritation for a more comfortable, soothing shave. The lotion-like texture takes a couple of shaves to get used to if you’ve traditionally used thicker shave creams or foams, but the feel of your skin during and after is immediately satisfying.

Shaving cream is often used as a catch-all term for several products that prep and protect your skin while you shave. There are three main types, and the right one depends on your razor, your skin type, and your personal preference.

If your shave is only as good as the cream you use, then the cream is only as good as its ingredients. Shaving creams often include soothing ingredients like aloe vera, which calms irritation and helps the skin stay hydrated before and after shaving. Shea butter is another popular one, as it provides rich moisture that softens hair and improves razor glide, reducing friction during the shave.

Many formulas also contain vitamin E, an antioxidant that nourishes the skin and supports repair after shaving. Then there is a slew of natural oils and other vitamins to keep an eye on, like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil that hydrate, soothe, and prevent post-shave irritation.

How often do you shave? That’s the most important question to ask yourself when considering the size of your cream. A larger tube offers better value and lasts longer, especially for daily shavers. I rock a beard most of the time, so I only shave for touch-ups on my neck and cheeks. Plus, I rarely shave body hair and stick to trimming. Because of this, I can often get away with a smaller tube. But if you’re clean-cut or shave large parts of your body, you’ll want to look to larger options.

#5111. Coinbase Says 99% of Customer Crypto Is Offline and Out of Hackers’ Reach

Coinbase Says 99% of Customer Crypto Is Offline and Out of Hackers’ Reach

Coinbase is moving to reassure customers that what happened at Binance can’t easily happen there.

In a blog post Wednesday, the U.S. exchange said it wasn’t affected by last week’s hack of Binance, in which attackers drained about $6.4 billion from the rival exchange’s hot wallets.

Coinbase said it keeps more than 99% of customer assets in cold storage, meaning offline wallets that can’t be reached over the internet. It moves funds into internet-connected hot wallets only as customers need them.

The Binance incident “has understandably left customers asking” how Coinbase guards against a similar attack, the post said.

Coinbase laid out several layers of protection. Private keys for its cold wallets are split into pieces and never fully reassembled, even when signing transactions, and no single employee has standing access to the hot-wallet signing service. Strict limits cap how fast funds can move from cold to hot wallets, and unusual withdrawal spikes are held until staff review them. The exchange can also trigger “kill switches” that take signing keys offline entirely.

The company said it assumes employees will be targeted by phishing, so its controls are designed so that a stolen password, session or device can’t be used on its own, and sensitive actions require multiple approvals.

That focus on insiders carries weight for Coinbase. In May 2025, it disclosed that criminals had bribed overseas customer support agents to steal personal data on less than 1% of its monthly transacting users, then demanded a $20 million ransom that Coinbase refused to pay.

Last week, Coinbase said a security incident at analytics vendor Amplitude exposed contact data for a “small subset” of customers, though funds weren’t affected.

Coinbase also said customer assets are held 1:1 and aren’t lent out unless customers direct it to, and it reported $8.6 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $377 billion in assets on its platform as of Sept. 30. It flagged artificial intelligence as a fast-changing threat and pledged further security investment.

The Binance theft, which the FBI has attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, has rattled the industry. Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic found that the laundering spanned about 12,000 wallets in under four days, while stablecoin issuers froze about 44% of the haul.

Separately, Brazil’s Mercado Bitcoin halted withdrawals after a $40 million hack, and French bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa recently confirmed a cyberattack that led to a $133 million crypto theft.

#5110. Circle’s ARC token sale lifts earnings as lower yields weigh on USDC income

Circle is looking to payments fees and future staking rewards to diversify revenue as its core stablecoin business faces pressure from lower yields and growing competition.

Circle’s expansion beyond stablecoins supplied the biggest boost to its third-quarter earnings, as the company recognized $182 million in revenue from its ARC token presale, helping offset falling income from the reserves backing its flagship stablecoin, USDC.

The company reported diluted earnings per share of $0.84, up from $0.64 a year earlier and double analysts’ expectations of $0.42. Total revenue and reserve income rose 17% to $865 million. Without the ARC token sale, however, revenue would have fallen from a year earlier.

Circle shares were down 0.84% at $74.59 at 4:05 pm UTC on Nov. 4, according to Yahoo Finance.

The results capture a transition for Circle. Its established stablecoin business earns returns on the reserves backing USDC, tying income to interest rates and the amount of the token outstanding. Its newer businesses aim to earn from the payments and financial activity those digital dollars support.

Circle launched its payments network in May 2025 to connect financial institutions settling cross-border payments with stablecoins. Arc, its blockchain for financial applications, went live on public mainnet on Sept. 16, 2026. Its native token, ARC, is intended to support network security and governance as Arc moves toward proof of stake in 2027, while transaction fees are paid in USDC.

That contribution arrived as lower reserve yields outweighed growth in USDC balances. Average circulation increased 8% year over year, but the reserve return fell 61 basis points to 3.5%. Reserve income declined 8% to $657.6 million.

Interest rates were lower than a year earlier, despite a Federal Reserve rate hike in September. The Fed raised its benchmark range by a quarter percentage point to 3.75%–4% in September, although that remained below the 4%–4.25% range set a year earlier. Circle’s reserve return also edged up from 3.48% in the second quarter, but the earnings pressure reflected the lower year-over-year yield.

USDC ended September at $73.9 billion in circulation, while its share of the stablecoin market fell 1.83 percentage points to 27%.

Competition is also expanding. Open Standard’s Open USD was live on Solana by Sept. 30, with Coinbase, Mastercard, Shopify, Stripe and Visa as founding partners. The stablecoin model distributes reserve earnings to partners after a management fee, giving businesses another option for accessing stablecoins and sharing their economics.

Related: ARK buys $17M in Coinbase, Circle shares while trimming Bullish

ARC changed Circle’s earnings picture. Excluding ARC presale revenue, total revenue and reserve income were $683 million, down roughly 8% year over year. Reported adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose 85% to $317 million. Without the ARC contribution, adjusted EBITDA was approximately $135 million, down 21% from $171 million a year earlier.

Circle anticipates staking rewards after Arc transitions to proof of stake, which it targets for 2027. That would create another source of revenue, although it remains dependent on the network’s development.

Circle is also beginning to charge for some payments-network activity. Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Fox-Geen said on the earnings call that the company expected material CPN revenue in 2027. CEO Jeremy Allaire described Circle’s strategy as building connected networks, with growth in stablecoins, payments and blockchain applications reinforcing one another.

“This is not just about payments, and it is not just about digital dollars. It is about multiple compounding flywheels on one platform. Every new member, every new builder, and every new asset makes the whole platform more valuable,” Allaire said.

The company is also adjusting its workforce size. The earnings disclosures included a reduction affecting approximately 5% of employees, which Circle said was intended to align its organization with its operating model and strategic priorities.

#5108. 8 Best Hand Creams of 2026: 3-plus Years of Editor Testing and Reviews

From Joonbyrd to L’Occitane, here’s what formulas actually work.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ll be the first to admit it: I spend a copious amount of money on spa treatments and refining my at-home skincare routine. From my $78 Isdin sunscreen and Paula’s Choice Exfoliant to biweekly facials, my focus has always been on achieving clear, wrinkle-free skin without injections. But after chatting with double board-certified dermatologist Serena Mraz, MD, I realized that I’ve been neglecting my hands for far too long.

As a New Yorker, I take the subway several times a day for work, events, and to meet up with friends. I’m also a germaphobe and rely on hand sanitizer or harsh soap in office and restaurant bathrooms after riding the train. As a result, my hands are inevitably dry, dull, and rough. That's not exactly the look I’m going for as our beauty editor. It also doesn’t help that Dr. Mraz says cumulative sun damage, including dark spots and wrinkles, is one of the biggest culprits in showing my age. Wait, what do you mean my age didn’t pause during the pandemic? “Your skin records sun exposure like your car tallies mileage,” dermatologist Hadley King, MD, previously told me about how skincare changes in your 40s. “You can't turn back the odometer on your car, and you can't turn back sun damage from your skin."

Hand creams provide instant hydration and support the skin barrier, helping me achieve the baby-soft skin of my dreams. I’ve noticed that investing in my favorites lets me reapply less frequently and use a smaller amount of product, ultimately trimming my cost per use. It’s beauty math, ladies!

Creams, such as L'Occitane and Beau Domaine, are the thickest and most nourishing type of hand care products. Dr. Mraz is a fan of creams because they’re packed with more lipids than water, which helps deliver the best moisture. The downside is that they take longer to rub into your hands and across larger areas like your arms.

Ointments, such as Aquaphor and Vaseline, are versatile, fragrance-free moisturizers that relieve dryness without causing irritation, says dermatologist and clinical professor of dermatology Gary Goldenberg, MD. They’re made with petrolatum to keep your skin moist, which helps prevent wounds from drying out and forming a scab. These are especially useful when you have super cracked skin.

Lotions are thinner and more fluid than creams. Some are even runny, but don’t worry: the right lotions still restore moisture for instant relief and prevent dryness. Notably, our best overall pick—Joonbyrd Wonder·Land Hand Lotion—has a luxurious consistency that feels and smells like it belongs in a spa. It’s so enjoyable, I use it all over my body and notice instant hydration without leaving residue on my clothes.

The dermatologists I consulted recommend moisturizing ingredients glycerin, shea butter, and cocoa butter—they can be found in many of our suggestions, like Aquaphor and Juara.

Hyaluronic acid is another standout that acts as a moisture magnet, holding up to 1,000 times its weight in water. It’s so epic that dermatologists recently told me you can even use hyaluronic acid on your hair and scalp.

As our fragrance-obsessed beauty editor, I also factored in the scent profiles. While all of these hand creams smell good, I also highlighted the key notes that make each one stand out. Homecourt's five impressive aromas—ranging from roses to citrus and aromatic—and Juara's Bali-inspired coconut blend are some of my favorites. If scents aren’t your thing, opt for Nécessaire. What it lacks in aroma, it makes up for in skin-nourishing and soothing ingredients, including ceramides and niacinamide.

To kick off this evaluation process, I went directly to medical experts about their no-fail hand creams.

Our team has been writing about hand creams since 2023. As our beauty editor, I refined our testing methodologies for 2026 to help you avoid buyer's remorse.

I opened the testing pool to 16 hand creams, but only eight were worth the hype. So how did I select them? In addition to ensuring these picks align with dermatological guidance, I compared 2026 launches (Joonbyrd) with reliable heavy-hitters, like L’Occitane and CeraVe. I also rummaged through the Women’s Health beauty closet and slathered on these hand creams. I started with my hands and explored how they work on different parts of my body, like my rough knees, elbows, and feet.

To narrow the list further, I used these hand creams twice daily for five months. I adored our best overall pick so much that I used it for an entire month straight before even writing this story because it’s genuinely that good.

I didn’t want the hand cream application to feel like a mundane process. To help you actually finish your next tube of hand cream, I evaluated each contender’s sensory experience. These factors included fragrance, texture, absorption time, finish, and if they left any residue on my gloves and tech.

Lastly, I considered each item’s cost relative to its product size and quality of ingredients and effectiveness. This final list includes a mix of affordable, mid-range, and splurge-worthy picks that provide varying levels of hydration and other cosmetic-enhancing benefits like lightening age spots.

Ready to make dry hands a thing of the past? Look no further than these eight expert-approved hand creams worthy of a spot in your routine.

As our beauty editor, I’m constantly searching for the next big thing. My new undisputed no. 1 hand cream hails from the U.K. and it quickly became my all-time favorite recommendation. Joonbyrd was developed by dermatologist Alexis Granite, MD, who is certified in America and the U.K. Given her elite medical background—Dr. Granite was a clinical instructor at New York-Presbyterian/Weill-Cornell—my expectations for her line were high.

Joonbyrd offers two hand care products: the featured Wonder·Land Hand Lotion and the Confetti Sky Hand Treatment. TBH, the latter is compact and more travel-friendly, but I genuinely love the Hand Lotion so much that I apply it to my body. My picky, scent-averse mom also found the sophisticated warm and sweet gourmand notes appealing.

Aroma aside, the formulation and ingredient list are on point. The fast-absorbing, nourishing lotion is made with all my favorite heavy hitters: ceramides, amino acids, and niacinamide. They’re basically a trifecta of skincare goodness that repair my skin barrier and hydrate.

Joonbyrd says this hand lotion moisturizes for up to 48 hours. However, I’m a frequent handwasher, so I can’t speak to going two full days without soap and water on my skin. Personally, I noticed my hands felt softer after a week of consistent reapplication, and I can use this lotion twice daily afterward.

I initially tested it for one month straight before comparing it to other picks. (More on that shortly!) Since then, I’ve been reaching for it almost daily for a year. It offers long-lasting hydration and skin barrier support. Joonbyrd is so effective at leaving my skin softer and more supple that even acquaintances have noticed how soft my hands feel.

To ensure others received a fair assessment during the second month of my testing process, I evaluated how Joonbyrd compared with other options.

Joonbyrd wins over the French staple, as it’s lighter and features a modern formula that strengthens the skin barrier. L’Occitane remains a beauty classic, but if you want something new that you can apply all over your body, opt for Joonbyrd.

Go with the latter if you’re a price-conscious shopper or just super sensitive to scents. Hey, it happens to me during the spring and summer, so I totally get it! Joonbyrd is luxurious—the pretty packaging elevates my vanity setup, and the green, textured exterior helps prevent it from rolling off my table.

Joonbyrd is a non-sticky lotion that absorbs quickly, leaving no pesky residue on my belongings. It’s your best bet when your hands require barrier support and nourishment. On the flip side, Aquaphor feels heavy compared to Joonbyrd’s formulation, but not as greasy as Vaseline. (More on that soon—promise!)

Here’s where things get tougher. HomeCourt offers an aspirational, Insta-famous brand vibe, but with hydrating ingredients that enhance my skin. I also like HomeCourt partially because it offers five fragrances ranging from floral to aromatic and citrus. It provides just enough hydration after washing my dishes or hands. Woo! But if I could only own one hand cream, I’d opt for Joonbyrd since it’s cosmetically elegant and effective. FWIW, HomeCourt makes a body care collection if you prefer. I’m also so obsessed with the 2026 Skincare Award-winning Exfoliating Hand Soap.

Both hand creams provide ample skin-replenishing goodness. While the fragrance-free Nécessaire Hand Cream is helpful for anyone with a sensitive nose and skin, I do miss having access to the line’s signature scents at my disposal.

Overall, Joonbyrd is the best hand cream to beat in 2026. I’ll continue using this nourishing lotion for its standout ingredients, luxurious feeling, and impressive short- and long-term performance. Plus, the packaging is pretty and adds a fun, feminine touch to my vanity. The container has a nice weight and features a lightly cushioned textured green exterior to help prevent accidental slippage.

Read more: Meet the Only Hair Masks That Saved My Dull, Dry Strands

CeraVe makes a strong case that you don’t have to splurge to enjoy a solid hand cream. To start, it contains derm-approved and barrier-supporting ingredients, including niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, ceramides, and dimethicone. It also boasts a fragrance-free formula that doesn’t irritate my sensitive skin.

Although CeraVe describes it as a cream, the consistency reminds me of a custardy lotion that feels supple on my skin without the watered-down feeling of cheaper lotions. It also absorbs quickly and doesn’t tug my skin like richer creams when I rub my hands together.

I genuinely enjoy this hand cream and plan to keep it in my rotation. But here’s the caveat: It requires more frequent reapplication than thicker creams. But at just $10 a tube, it’s by far the most affordable recommendation, making it a major win in my book. Pick this hand cream if you’re shopping on a budget and don’t want to skimp on moisture and barrier repair.

Arguably the most famous hand cream of the bunch, L'Occitane's non-greasy formula has earned plenty of love from our beauty team. We previously featured this exact product in our at-home manicure tutorial and highlighted the brand in our Skincare Awards and guides to the best spa-worthy bodycare products.

So what makes it so iconic? L’Occitane is made with gentle, effective ingredients, such as 20 percent organic shea butter, glycerin, and skin-plumping omegas. The consistency is thick enough to keep my hands hydrated overnight, yet it absorbs relatively fast enough that it won't leave a trail on my keyboard.Before I wrote about beauty for nine years, I was a tad excessive with products. The trick is that less is truly more with this South of France staple, and find the ideal amount for you, which varies based on your environment and how active you’ve been with your hands. I like to squeeze out a few pea-sized drops to start, then add more as needed to avoid leaving a heavy, mask-like feeling.I also can’t get over the enticing aroma. It reminds me of a high-end French soap with a soft, almost baby-powder-like aroma, and a touch of warmth from shea butter and almond.

Since Courteney Cox launched Homecourt in 2022, the brand’s stylish design and hydrating formula elevate handcare into a sensory experience that I always look forward to using. While I’m all in on her All-Purpose Spray, it’s her splurge-worthy Hand Wash and Hand Cream that seal the deal for me.

For starters, it’s the only pick that comes in a sleek black pump, adding a minimal chic touch to my bathroom and kitchen sinks. But what truly shines—and has me buying in bulk—is the velvety-soft texture that absorbs quickly like a lotion but nourishes my hands like a cream. Shea butter is the star that helps condition and soften my skin, while Australian hibiscus flower extract hydrates and protects, and microalgae oil nourishes. The formula quenches my dry hands after washing and drying dishes, and the texture dries down fast without feeling goopy.And sure, all hand creams on this list smell good, but Homecourt truly excels at scents. Cece, Cox's signature scent, opens up with aromatic notes of Guatemalan cardamom, dried mate absolute leaves, Sri Lankan cinnamon, and carrot. It also features Indonesian patchouli and vetiver oil.Another standout: Cipres Mint, a mix of Chinese eucalyptus oil and spearmint (naturally!) with black tea, Texan white cedarwood, and dried Indian papyrus. My handcare routine and entire home smell like Cipres Mint, and I always get compliments from houseguests. If you’re more into floral aromas, there’s Steeped Rose, while citrus fans can gravitate toward Mandarin Basile and Neroli Leaf.Truthfully, I love Homecourt products and have gifted many hand cream and hand soap sets to loved ones over the years. If I had to nitpick, it would be an improvement if Homecourt sold refills for the hand cream, as they do for the Hand Wash and Surface Cleaner. However, those are liquids in a 1-liter paper pouch that probably couldn’t handle the cream’s thicker consistency.

As our team’s resident Nécessaire fan, I just had to introduce you to this fragrance-free hand cream. It’s my go-to when my hands are feeling extra sensitive, or during allergy season, when my nose itches and my eyes water at scents. The fast-absorbing hand cream is made without pesky silicones and parabens that could trigger my eczema.

Above all, I appreciate that it’s enriched with niacinamide, plus shea and marula butters for instant skin comfort without the heavy feeling of other similar products. The Hand Cream is also made with marula oil, five types of ceramides for hydration, and vitamin E for an antioxidant boost. Its pH-balanced formula also contains vitamin C to help prevent skin dullness.While I’m totally into the fragrance-free scent, Nécessaire is known for its array of enticing aromas. Currently, there are no scented versions of this hand cream, so if that’s a deal breaker for you, then it’s best to skip this suggestion.

Aquaphor and Vaseline are similar drugstore staples—they both use petroleum to lock in moisture and repair the skin barrier. But Aquaphor takes the edge since it contains humectants to draw water to the skin for additional hydration, dermatologist Alicia Zalka, MD, previously told us. It’s made with a mineral oil called paraffinum liquidum and a wax called ceresin. There’s also soothing bisabolol, and a blend of hydrating glycerin, lanolin, and panthenol.

Since Aquaphor contains more ingredients than Vaseline, it hits the moisturizing trifecta by acting as an occlusive (a thick, protective layer), emollient (trapping moisture in the skin), and humectant (drawing in hydration). It’s not the most exciting product on this list, but it’s certainly effective and ideal for someone who prefers a no-frills routine. Aquaphor also creates a protective barrier between your skin and the elements during high-altitude skiing and snowboarding sessions.

Need another reason to hit “add to cart”? Aquaphor is thicker, waxier, and less greasy than Vaseline, making it comfier to apply to my hands. Like the Embryolisse Lait-Crème Concentré, this ointment can be applied to other areas of skin, including chapped lips or dry nostrils. However, it’s not as multitasking as Lait-Créme, which can be used in six ways versus three. More on that shortly!

Ultimately, you can’t go wrong with Aquaphor, especially since it’ll only set you back just under-$13 for a massive 7 oz tube of ointment. While it might be a tad inconvenient for your daily purse, it’s still worth ordering. Given its large size, you won’t misplace it like with other smaller hand creams and lip balms like I inevitably do. Plus, if you’re feeling generous then you can share with your partner or family without worrying about running low for the foreseeable future.

Dermatologist Nicole Ruth, DO, and the Women’s Health beauty team are all big fans of Brad Pitt’s hand cream, but don’t let the celebrity association fool you. We named Beau Domaine the best hand cream in our 2025 Skincare Awards, and it’s still an essential part of our routines in 2026.

Beau Domaine packs a powerful beauty punch by blending luxury with science, says Dr. Ruth. She points to the grape-derived antioxidants and deeply nourishing moisturizers—shea butter and organic olive oil—that improve both the feel and appearance of your hands.

Most options simply hydrate, but this luxurious hand cream visibly reduces discoloration and refines uneven skin texture, leaving it more luminous. The rich texture also nourishes my hands and softens my cuticles, making it a must before manicures. Given its TSA-friendly size, it’s also a must-have during my in-flight beauty routine.While the upfront cost is a bit jarring, Beau Domaine’s dual-action formula justifies the cost. The combination of science-backed ingredients, Dr. Ruth’s endorsement, and our coveted Skincare Awards seal of approval fully justifies the cost. Plus, her patients consistently comment that Beau Domaine absorbs quickly, leaves zero greasiness, and gives an immediate smoothing effect while still feeling elegant and silky.

Deal with itchy, scaly hands? You’ll need something offering more intensive hydration without compromising on gentle components. Dr. Ruth recommends this hand cream and says it’s a popular pick among her patients with eczema.

The New York-based doctor points to the rich ingredients, such as candlenut oil, illipe butter, and turmeric, which provide long-lasting moisture and antioxidant protection. It’s also made with coconut oil, which locks in moisture for overnight hydration. Mangosteen butter gives it a custard-like texture that delivers ample hydration like a cream, but blends easily like a balm.

Another reason I appreciate the texture: It absorbs quickly—I can text quickly or flip through channels without leaving behind residue. The earthy brown tube of Juara lives on my nightstand, and after using it on and off for three months, I can confirm it blends and nourishes like a dream with zero residue.

Though Juara doesn't make any specific eczema safety certifications, Dr. Ruth doesn’t mind it for her patients with that skin condition. TBH, my eczema flares up during the winter and seasonal transitions, but this nourishing cream hasn’t caused any sensitivity issues.

Embryolisse is a French pharmacy staple trusted by our beauty team and the lead makeup artist on Emily in Paris. Most know Lait-Crème Concentré as a face moisturizer and makeup primer—it leaves my skin dewy even after using retinol—but it functions six ways, including as a hand cream. Wait, what? Mhmmm, I apply a small pea-sized amount of Lait-Crème Concentré to hydrate my hands without feeling greasy or sticky. Chock-full of shea butter and soothing aloe vera, my hands look visibly hydrated and luminous. I rub it into my hands and get back to typing on my laptop or phone within a minute.

With holiday travel coming up, carry-on space is limited and valuable. Think of Lait-Crème Concentré as the Swiss Army knife of skincare. It works as a moisturizing face mask, after-sun treatment, shaving cream, and cleansing milk—yup, just add a little water for a hydrating wash. This lightweight cream also helps minimize my retinol-related flaking and redness.TBH, I like pretty much everything about this multipurpose hand cream. The only con is that the larger size is currently out of stock on Amazon. Still, at just $19 for an icon from the French pharmacy, you can’t go wrong, especially since you won’t deal with VAT refunds at CDG Airport in Paris.

#5102. Google Tells Schools They Can Reject AI—But They'll Lose Search, Too

Google Tells Schools They Can Reject AI—But They'll Lose Search, Too

Google is giving schools more freedom to reject artificial intelligence—provided they're also willing to give up Google Search, which is arguably what everybody in the world uses Google for.

The company announced Tuesday that its AI products will be disabled by default for K-12 student accounts unless administrators explicitly enable them. But schools that want to ban AI entirely will also have to disable Google's search engine, a tool millions of students rely on for everyday research.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, tried to justify the reasoning during a meeting with educators.

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” he said according to Education Week. Schools uncomfortable with AI can choose not to enable Search at all.

Google says administrators will be able to activate or disable Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search individually. That means schools can block the standalone chatbots while keeping Search available, but they cannot remove AI from Search itself.

For teachers who want students to research sources without receiving AI-generated answers, the company is effectively offering two options: accept its AI-powered search or find another search engine.

The announcement is already drawing accusations that Google is using its dominance in education to push a technology many schools are still trying to understand, regulate or restrict.

Google says the changes are intended to address concerns that AI chatbots can undermine learning by giving students ready-made answers instead of encouraging them to solve problems themselves.

Beginning in early 2027, schools that enable Search will be offered versions with conventional AI features, such as AI Overviews and AI Mode, or the education-focused Guided Learning experience, according to The New York Times.

Neither option provides the traditional search experience without generative AI.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the company of “trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” according to CBS News.

Former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan was equally critical, accusing Google of using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI.

The criticism comes as some of America's largest school districts are actively restricting generative AI. New York City, for example, imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI through eighth grade, covering nearly 600,000 students, while Los Angeles has also restricted the technology.

Los Angeles officials had specifically hoped to preserve Google Search while removing AI-generated summaries. Under the newly announced controls, that won't be an option.

Google's position also arrives amid continuing antitrust scrutiny. A federal court ruled in 2024 that Google unlawfully monopolized the U.S. search market, and the company has faced separate legal challenges over its decision to integrate AI summaries into search results.

School administrators are expected to receive the new controls in early 2027. They will be able to decide which AI products students can access, and even apply different settings by grade level. A Google Search option without AI, however, is not among the choices.

That said, for schools that want to, ahem, unofficially ban AI without losing Google search, our guide may provide a quick solution. It takes 5 minutes and lasts forever.

#5101. Riot shares surge on $28B AI lease as Hut 8 sinks on revenue miss

Bitcoin miner Riot sold BTC to finance its AI expansion, while Hut 8 reported falling revenue and rising costs before its major data center leases generate income.

Shares of Bitcoin miner Riot Platforms surged more than 13% Wednesday after the company announced a $28 billion AI data center lease, its largest agreement to date as it accelerates its expansion into artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The 15-year agreement covers 910 megawatts at its Corsicana, Texas, facility, bringing its total future contracted data center revenue to approximately $38 billion across three leases signed this year. The agreement represents a major step in Riot’s AI infrastructure strategy as it moves away from relying primarily on Bitcoin mining revenue.

“A year ago, our cash flow depended on the price of Bitcoin, and now, at full deployment of currently executed deals, nearly all of our expected cash flow will be generated from long-term leases with leading players in the AI ecosystem,” CEO Jason Les said during Wednesday’s earnings call.

According to Riot’s third-quarter earnings release, Riot will provide land and power infrastructure originally developed for Bitcoin mining, while the AI tenant, identified as Anthropic in the company’s quarterly filing, will own and operate the computing equipment and cover operating expenses.

Riot estimates the project’s total capital costs at $5.5 billion, financed primarily through debt backed by lease payments, although financing has not yet been secured. The first phase is expected to be delivered in September 2027, with rental payments beginning within 60 days of delivery.

Riot also reported third-quarter revenue of $181.4 million, up just 1% year over year, and sold 10,599 BTC during the quarter to help finance its data center expansion. During Wednesday’s earnings call, CEO Jason Les said Bitcoin mining at Corsicana could begin winding down in summer 2027.

Related: Bitcoin miners face widening AI financing costs as lenders scrutinize deals

Meanwhile, shares of fellow Bitcoin miner Hut 8 plunged more than 22% at one point on Wednesday after the company reported weaker-than-expected quarterly revenue amid its transition toward AI infrastructure.

Third-quarter revenue fell 15% to $71.1 million, missing analysts’ estimates of $75.8 million, according to MarketBeat data. During Wednesday’s earnings call, CFO Sean Glennan attributed the decline partly to asset sales and lower revenue per Bitcoin mined, while cash administrative expenses also rose year over year.

“The legacy revenue base is no longer the main growth driver, while the larger contracted infrastructure revenues remain tied to delivery milestones,” Glennan said.

CEO Asher Genoot also pointed to the complexity and expense of traditional AI data center construction as the company looks to develop projects on a larger scale.

“Many of today’s data centers resemble NASA rocket programs—remarkable engineering, but complex, expensive, and slow to deliver,” Genoot said.

According to the company’s third-quarter earnings presentation, Hut 8 has already secured $7.5 billion in project bonds to fully finance two major AI data center developments, although neither has begun generating lease revenue.

#5099. I Tried Two New Therabody Devices. Now I Have a Tension-Melting Routine

Combining heat, massage, and targeted percussive therapy helps me decompress from the day.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I carry my stress in my shoulders and my neck. I always have. It’s the last quarter of the year, when my job responsibilities tend to ramp up, and my family responsibilities have increased this year, too. Recently, I started running regularly again to help find some me-time, but instead of releasing tension, the activity has left my traps and neck stiff. No amount of meditation or yoga is releasing these burdens that have nested into my shoulders, upper back, and neck.

Luckily, Therabody needed someone to try its newest massagers: ThermNeck & Upper Back and ThermFace Massage. I was their girl. Full disclosure: I’m a Theragun fan. It’s been helping me recover from workouts and race training for years. Products that target my stress zone sounded promising—and much-needed. I love my Theragun, but it can be unwieldy when I try to reach those areas myself. So I began working the two Therabody massagers into my after-work wellness routine. Here’s how it went.

First, I started with ThermFace Massage. When I initially heard about it, I wasn’t sure what to expect—or whether I’d like it. I live with migraine, so I was cautious about the prospect of vibration around my head.

ThermFace Massage may look just like a smaller Theragun, but it isn’t. It’s Therabody’s first heated percussive massage device specifically engineered to handle the delicate muscles of the face, jaw, and neck. It has 5-millimeter amplitude, three speeds, three heat levels, and four specialized attachments—Heat, Cone, Dampener, and Wedge—that allows you to customize the experience. And unlike the Theragun, ThermFace Massage has a 45-degree ergonomic shape that makes it easier to navigate all contours of the jaw, face, and neck.

The first time I used it, I chose the softest attachment and started on the right side of my neck. I turned it on at the lowest speed and moved slowly, paying close attention to how my body responded. The sensation was targeted but not aggressive. Once I felt comfortable, I guided it along the muscles of my jaw, where I hadn’t fully realized I was holding tension.

That became my first lesson: Stress doesn’t always announce itself. Sometimes it shows up as a clenched jaw during a difficult email, a tight face at the end of a long day, or stiffness that seems to travel from the jaw into the neck.

Next, I tested the heat attachment. ThermFace Massage offers three temperature settings ranging from 40°C to 55°C. This allowed me start conservatively rather than jump straight to the warmest option, which has since become my favorite setting. The combination of adjustable heat and focused percussion made the routine feel purposeful: I’m taking care of my overlooked, overworked muscles.

Because I live with migraine, I remain deliberate about where and how I use the device, but I haven’t experienced an increase in episodes while using ThermFace Massage. Anyone managing a health condition should check with a medical professional before introducing a new device into their routine, as I did before I started this trial.

Next came the ThermNeck & Upper Back, a cordless wearable designed to target the neck, trapezius muscles, and upper back. If ThermFace Massage helped me notice how much tension I carried around my jaw, ThermNeck & Upper Back went straight to the place where I already knew my stress lived.

It combines five complementary therapies in one device: kneading massage, heat, far-infrared, near-infrared LED light, and Theragun percussive therapy. Two built-in Theraguns are positioned over the trapezius muscles (located in the upper back), and the device includes three percussive speeds, three kneading patterns, and three heat levels.

I slipped it over my shoulders while seated on my sofa and used the adjustable strap to fine-tune the placement and pressure. It’s wearable, but not completely hands-free; resting my hands in the straps allowed me to control how firmly the device sat against my muscles.

That adjustability mattered. After a run, I may want a different intensity than I do after eight hours at my computer. Some evenings, I’m looking for targeted percussion. On others, soothing heat and kneading massage are more appealing. Depending on what my body needs on a given day, I can tailor my time with the device.

ThermNeck & Upper Back should be used while seated or standing, not while lying down. I found sitting on the sofa to be the ideal setup—comfortable enough to decompress, but upright enough to keep the device properly positioned.

Now when I get home from work, I change into comfy clothes, make dinner for my family, then slip on ThermNeck & Upper Body and watch television while the device kneads away the stress of the day that has built up in my neck and upper back. Five minutes is all it takes to transition from responsibility mode to evening mode, making me more relaxed and calm for the time that means the most to me: family time.

The hour before bed, I brush my teeth, wash my face, use my TheraFace Mask Glo (told you I was a Therabody fan), then retire to my bed. There, I use the ThermFace Massage (usually the Heat attachment) to massage my jaw and neck for a couple of minutes on each side, followed by reading and then sleep.

While none of the devices will erase my deadlines or family obligations, they do help with my running-related stiffness and ease the tension in the places where those pressures land. This routine has also created a better awareness around my head, neck, and shoulders: Am I clenching my jaw? Are my shoulders creeping toward my ears? Have I moved away from my screen recently?

Meditation and yoga still have a place in my life. But sometimes my stress feels less like a thought I can breathe through and more like a knot sitting directly on top of my shoulders. This new routine allows me to use targeted heat and massage to help loosen that knot with a few intentional minutes at the end of the day.

Fleece is a soft, synthetic fabric usually made from a polyester blend, often mixed with spandex, nylon, or cotton. Designed to mimic wool's insulating properties, fleece is lighter, more breathable, and dries faster, making it ideal for staying warm. Plus, fleece wicks away moisture and dries quickly, keeping you cozy even if you’re caught in rain or snow. Think of it like wearing a warm hug on a cold day.

When it comes to fleece leggings, the fabric blend is key. Most leggings are made from a mix of polyester and spandex, which delivers the perfect blend of warmth, stretch, and comfort. We’ll give you a quick breakdown of why these materials are key here:

Polyester traps heat, making it an ideal blend for staying warm without bulk. Compared to natural fibers like cotton, polyester dries quickly. WH editors love wearing polyester-fleece leggings on long walks since they stay warm without making you feel sweaty. It’s super lightweight yet strong, meaning you won’t feel like the material is clinging to your body. Polyester also helps leggings retain their shape over time, so stretching, sagging, and pilling are likely a thing of the past.

Nylon is a popular material in fleece leggings because of its strength, flexibility, and smooth texture. It resists wear and tear, which helps keep leggings looking brand new after every wash. Nylon also offers water resistance, which is key for outdoor activities in light rain or snow.

Spandex (also known as elastane or Lycra) is the go-to fabric for stretch and flexibility. It fits snugly and moves with you, giving you maximum comfort during high-impact activities like yoga, running, and dance. While it’s not as durable on its own, spandex is often blended with other fabrics (like nylon or polyester) to create leggings that are both stretchy and long-lasting.

Here’s the thing: Fleece leggings with thicker fabric may feel more restrictive than traditional leggings, so if you plan to wear them for high-impact activities, opting for a bigger size might be best. Look for four-way stretch fabrics like spandex for flexibility and comfort. If you're between sizes, choose based on your desired fit—size down for a sculpted look (read: tighter) or up for a relaxed, lounge-friendly feel.

Fleece leggings are perfect for workouts, offering warmth and insulation while keeping the stretch and comfort you need for full range of motion. “The leggings should have a good amount of stretch while fitting snugly, and maintaining their shape throughout the day,” says fashion designer Kadeem Alphanso Fyffe. Look for features like a wide, high-rise waistband for a secure fit.

We analyzed everything from fabric quality and warmth to stretch, fit, and breathability. Were they soft and supportive? Did they hold their shape after multiple washes? #5096. Trump-linked tokens lead crypto losses after Democrats sweep in the US midterms

The official Trump and World Liberty Financial tokens were the two biggest losers among the top 100 cryptocurrencies on Wednesday, even as Bitcoin and Ether rallied.

Two crypto tokens linked to US President Donald Trump led losses among the top 100 digital assets on Wednesday following the US midterm elections, raising questions about their future as the broader crypto market rallied.

Official Trump (TRUMP) fell 17% over 24 hours to $1.33, while World Liberty Financial (WLFI) dropped over 7% to $0.047, according to CoinMarketCap data from around 5:32 pm UTC. TRUMP is the president’s official memecoin, launched in January 2025, while WLFI is the governance token of World Liberty Financial, a Trump family-backed decentralized finance (DeFi) project launched in 2024.

The declines followed a wave of Democratic victories, including surprise wins in Texas, in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with the party winning control of both the House and Senate from Republicans.

The results could not only make it harder for Trump to push forward his crypto plans but also bring more scrutiny to his family’s crypto businesses. Analysts say the losses also raise questions about whether political sentiment alone can fuel demand for Trump-linked tokens.

Bitcoin (BTC) rose more than 4% over 24 hours to around $80,500, while Ether (ETH) climbed 6% to $2,433, according to CoinMarketCap data. Other major cryptocurrencies also posted gains, with BNB rising 3%, XRP climbing 2.6% and Solana (SOL) gaining 2.5%. The overall crypto market rose 3.4% to $2.69 trillion.

Meanwhile, the losses extended to other Trump family-linked tokens, such as the MELANIA memecoin, associated with First Lady Melania Trump. MELANIA dropped nearly 13% over 24 hours to around $0.066.

A separate token named after Vice President JD Vance (VANCE) also dropped nearly 12%, although it has no confirmed official connection to the vice president.

The losses were further reflected across the broader political memecoin market, with the sector’s total market capitalization falling more than 16% on the day to $477 million. Trading volume jumped 123% to $437 million, per CoinMarketCap data.

Related: US midterm elections 2026 as it happened: Democrats win control of Congress

Benjamin Sarquis Peillard, founder and CEO of Cap, a DeFi platform focused on stablecoin yields, told Cointelegraph that investors appear to be treating politically linked tokens differently from other cryptocurrencies.

“Bitcoin and other established assets respond to a combination of liquidity, institutional flows and macroeconomic conditions, while politically linked tokens can be more sensitive to shifts in expectations around Washington,” he said. “Even as the broader market recovers, those tokens may face selling pressure if investors begin reassessing their risk exposure.”

And while the selloff could be indicative of a short-term reaction to the election results, Peillard said the “longer-term question is what supports demand for these tokens beyond their association with a political figure.”

Beyond the market reaction, the election results also raise questions about the future of US crypto legislation, including the currently stalled Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, commonly referred to as the CLARITY Act.

The bill, which aims to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets, failed to advance in the Senate earlier this year after falling short of the 60 votes required. Democrats were pushing for stronger ethical provisions and safeguards against conflicts of interest involving Trump’s crypto ventures — four Republicans also opposed advancing the legislation.

“The midterm results introduce a new layer of regulatory uncertainty, particularly around the pace and direction of digital asset legislation,” Peillard said. “For politically linked tokens, that uncertainty can have a more immediate impact because investor sentiment is partly tied to expectations around the political environment.”

While the crypto sector continues to have support — and opposition — from lawmakers in both parties, it remains to be seen how the election results will affect crypto legislation.

Peillard said that for the broader industry, the “more important question is whether Congress can establish a durable regulatory framework that provides clarity regardless of which party holds power.”
